author: Zijing Wu
article_content:
The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linked to Alice Huang was a sprawling web of companies between Nvidia and China-based users of its chips that included cloud computing partners, online gaming tycoons, Cambodian traffickers and hundreds of shell companies, the FT found.

These seemingly unconnected enterprises combined — without necessarily being aware of the full picture — to make billions of dollars from one of the most profitable illicit trades in the world: moving Nvidia chips into China.

The FT traced the connections after speaking to more than a dozen people with knowledge of the operations, revealing links that were obscured by complex structures through hundreds of corporate filings.

Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial in developing cutting-edge AI and have become a vital commodity in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.

Washington’s export controls to prevent Beijing from acquiring the most powerful processors have created a multibillion-dollar black market to circumvent US curbs and satisfy China’s insatiable demand.

“Chip smuggling isn’t different from drugs or arms in terms of the structure of the supply chain. But there’s this importance attached to the semiconductor industry — it’s how the US wants to delay China in the AI race,” said Chris Clague, an associate fellow at International Institute for Strategic Studies who has focused on illicit trades in the past decade.

Moving advanced chips into China requires three main corporate channels: a group that is permitted to acquire and distribute the semiconductors; customers that do not fall foul of US export restrictions; and an underground network to smuggle the goods into China and money out.

The network linked to Alice Huang reached the US through Inspur, which was one of Nvidia’s largest partners for assembling chips into ready-to-use servers in China.

In March of 2023, Inspur was added to the US “entity list” for allegedly assisting the Chinese military. Some of its affiliates were also added to the register — but not Inspur’s part-owned US subsidiary, based in San Jose, California.

Inspur renamed the US unit Aivres, and since it was not on the entity list, it was able to keep trading with Nvidia.

Inside the chipmaker, there were questions about whether Aivres should qualify as an original equipment manufacturing (OEM) partner because of its links to Inspur, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. But Nvidia concluded the company met all compliance and export control requirements.

The second plank of the network was a customer that met the requirements to buy Nvidia chips at scale. OEM partners such as Aivres, which are allowed to integrate Nvidia GPUs into systems and sell those on, still needed to prove that their customers are not Chinese to access the US chipmaker’s products.

To be a qualified end customer, Nvidia requires at least three years of corporate records and proof that its management and owners are not majority Chinese.

Seeking to regain access to chip supplies, some of Inspur’s Chinese clients sought help from a successful online gaming company, Century Huatong, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter.

Over two decades, the Chinese group had morphed from a car parts business into a gaming platform, finally emerging as a data centre investor with deep connections in the industry.

Century Huatong veterans discussed ways to gain access to the chips with its associates and business partners. The solution that emerged involved using an offshore shell company that would not trigger US export restrictions and could be branded as a “neocloud” provider.

That shell became Megaspeed, while Alice Huang fulfilled the requirement for a “trusted” outward-facing executive with a spotless record, according to people with knowledge of the arrangement.

Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, was an early investor in Century Huatong, according to Chinese corporate filings. His fund Hexi Investment also backed a 2020 Century Huatong data centre project with 7Road, a Shenzhen-based gaming company in which both Huang and Century Huatong had invested.

Alice Huang and Kang Wei did not respond to requests for comment.

7Road International, the offshore arm of 7Road, was the forerunner of Megaspeed, having had several years of clean corporate records in Singapore. In 2023, Huang acquired its unit in the city-state and renamed it.

An Nvidia spokesperson said: “We placed Megaspeed and a subsidiary on our block list in 2025 . . . we do not sell to them, and if one of our OEM customers identifies the company for any planned shipment, we do not approve the OEM sale.” Nvidia added that it had also restricted sales to Aivres.

Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment but has previously said that it “conducts legitimate and lawful business”.

With her English skills, Hong Kong residency and reputation as a good networker and dealmaker, Huang was seen as an ideal western-friendly representative, according to people who knew her at the time.

It also helped that she and her husband were already looking to move into data centre businesses in south-east Asia that would lease chips to Chinese tech companies.

“Alice was chosen [to lead Megaspeed] because of the trust built over years,” said a person who had business dealings with her around the time.

The third — and essential — element of the enterprise was finding a partner to move chips into China.

People familiar with the matter said that Hu Xiaowei, who US authorities say is a leading figure in a Cambodia-based syndicate sanctioned for cyber scams and money laundering, filled at least part of this role.

Hu, who was arrested in Japan in the summer, could not be reached for comment. He has been accused by US authorities of running smuggling and gambling rings as the “second-in-command” at Prince Group.

A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu has never worked for the business and there was “no evidence of the US government’s unsupported allegations”.

Hu made money from online gaming-related businesses that brought him into contact with Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

The connections between Hu and Century Huatong run through a complex web of shareholdings and an IP partnership spanning dozens of company records examined by the FT.

Some content could not load. Check your internet connection or browser settings.

One clear link can be traced through Wang Ji, Century Huatong’s chair and largest individual shareholder, who was the majority owner of a now-dissolved Ningxia-based company where Hu served as a director.

Another director of the dissolved company owns a Chongqing-based firm that controls multiple gaming entities associated with Fang Zhizhen, whom the US has sanctioned for allegedly laundering money for Prince Group. Prince Group’s spokesperson said there was no evidence of a connection between Fang and the group.

Century Huatong’s ties to the alleged Prince Group leadership date back to about 2015, when the gaming platform began a process to ultimately acquire Shanda Games, owner of the Chinese rights to the viral game Legend of Mir in a landmark $4.2bn transaction.

Hu and his associates were involved in a group that hosted the Legend of Mir games on private servers, a hugely profitable business. Several members were arrested in 2016 for IP infringement, a case recently overturned due to corruption within the investigation, according to state media reports.

Around the time of the arrests, Hu moved to Cambodia, according to two people from the online gaming industry who knew him.

Online games are commonly used for money laundering because virtual currencies or in-game items can be bought with illicit funds and then sold on the secondary market to make the money appear legitimate.

The games groups have also long been in Nvidia’s orbit: before the chipmaker shifted focus to power the AI industry in 2022, the biggest demand for its GPUs in China was for gaming and crypto.

“If you look at the people and entities involved in today’s chip smuggling, lots of familiar names are from online gaming back in the day,” said a person who was involved in gaming deals.

“Many of them developed ‘grey’ side businesses such as money laundering and already built the infrastructure onshore and offshore to move money and goods around,” the person added.

Prince Group’s alleged “grey” infrastructure, some of the most extensive in the region, ranged from elaborate shell company structures to underground financing channels via online games and crypto, according to the people familiar with its operations.

The Prince Group spokesperson said it did not “have an illicit network” and there was “no foundation for claiming the existence of one, other than the unsupported US allegations in an indictment already proven to be riddled with falsehoods and temporal impossibilities”.

The group is also alleged to have physically smuggled goods via a fleet of private and business jets purchased by Hong Kong-based aircraft leasing companies that Hu founded, the people said. The Prince Group spokesperson said the allegation “has zero factual basis”.

By mid-2023, the elements were in place for the rise of Megaspeed. It officially approached Nvidia, pitching itself as a neocloud company with data centres in Malaysia and a leasing contract with Alibaba.

Led by Huang, Megaspeed passed the chipmaker’s compliance checks and quickly became one of its largest clients in the region.

Along the way, Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang, according to multiple industry insiders. Her nickname in the Chinese data centre circles was “Jensen’s personal assistant”.

At Megaspeed, business was booming. The declared value of goods imported from Aivres by Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, was about $4.6bn between December 2024 and December 2025, according to ImportGenius trade data.

Many of those chips ended up in China, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter. A raid by Indonesian police in early 2026 found empty server racks with no GPUs at the local Megaspeed subsidiary, according to Singapore’s Straits Times.

Multiple people involved in chip distribution channels said that once the Nvidia products passed through smuggling routes in south-east Asia — a process that can involve multiple countries and take weeks — they moved to the black market in China, where they were sold at multiples of their original price.

Once the chips were inside China, one of the key distributors of the smuggled Nvidia chips in the country was Shanghai Century Litong, which was established by a subsidiary of Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the transactions. The Information first reported Century Litong’s role in the network of Nvidia chip trade in China.

Corporate filings suggest Alice Huang was again linked to the formation of the group. With her sister, Huang Yu, she controlled an investment vehicle that had a joint venture with Century Huatong called Shanghai Century Longteng.

Longteng later founded Century Litong. Bloomberg reported that restricted Nvidia chips were found in Longteng-related data centres in Shanghai.

The FT revealed last year that at least $1bn worth of smuggled Nvidia chips were sold in China in just three months after President Trump tightened controls on H20, a less powerful chip made for the Chinese market to meet export control requirements.

People with knowledge of the smuggling operations say the layers of corporations were set up to mask the flow of AI chips into China. They also provided a useful buffer between the smuggling entities and the end users — some of which are China’s biggest tech groups.

Tencent and Alibaba, two of China’s biggest tech companies, both have business ties with Century Huatong. Tencent, China’s largest social media, messaging and gaming platform, has a 10.1 per cent stake in the company.

Century Huatong, through its fully owned subsidiary, invested in T3 Travel, a car-hailing business that also counts both Tencent and Alibaba as investors. Alice Huang is on the board of T3.

The FT has found no evidence to suggest that Tencent or Alibaba were involved in the chip smuggling businesses. Tencent said: “We are minority investors in a variety of internet and video game companies. We have no connection to nor knowledge of the other activities alleged in the story.”

Alibaba did not respond to a request for comment.

Inspur, Aivres, Century Huatong, 7Road, Shanghai Century Litong and Shanghai Century Longteng also did not respond to requests for comment.

Two US administrations have tried to protect the country’s lead over China in AI by restricting access to Nvidia’s most advanced processors. This week, the Trump administration announced further limits on how Chinese companies can access the chips via south-east Asia.

But it was US export controls that opened up a lucrative opportunity for those willing to break the rules, said Hanna Dohmen, senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

“When there’s a significant demand not met, you get smuggling,” said Dohmen. “We need to be realistic about what export controls can achieve. It doesn’t mean no US chip will make its way to China. When you put a lid on south-east Asia, would they not just go to other countries?”

Additional reporting from Eleanor Olcott in Beijing, Michael Acton in San Francisco and Owen Walker in Singapore.

title_zh: 英伟达高端芯片非法走私链调查
summary_zh: 前Megaspeed高管Alice Huang被曝卷入通过空壳公司网络向中国走私英伟达芯片的非法贸易链
article_content_zh:
英国《金融时报》调查发现，这位与英伟达前首席执行官黄仁勋有恋爱关系的中国女商人与供应人工智能芯片的网络有联系，其中包括一家涉嫌柬埔寨犯罪企业。

Megaspeed 前高管 Alice Huang 是美国调查英伟达在东南亚最大客户是否参与地下芯片交易的核心人物。一些美国官员怀疑黄爱丽是中国间谍，北京方面将这一说法斥为“诽谤”。

英国《金融时报》发现，与爱丽丝黄有联系的是英伟达及其芯片中国用户之间的庞大公司网络，其中包括云计算合作伙伴、在线游戏大亨、柬埔寨毒贩和数百家空壳公司。

这些看似毫无联系的企业联合起来——不一定了解全局——从世界上最赚钱的非法交易之一中赚取了数十亿美元：将英伟达芯片转移到中国。

英国《金融时报》在与十多名了解运营情况的人士交谈后追踪了这些联系，通过数百份公司文件揭示了被复杂结构掩盖的联系。

英伟达的先进芯片对于开发尖端人工智能至关重要，并已成为中美地缘政治竞争中的重要商品。

华盛顿为阻止北京收购最强大的加工商而实施的出口管制创造了价值数十亿美元的黑市，以规避美国的限制并满足中国永不满足的需求。

“就供应链结构而言，芯片走私与毒品或武器没有什么不同。但半导体行业有其重要性——这就是美国希望在人工智能竞赛中拖延中国的方式，”国际战略研究所副研究员克里斯·克拉格（Chris Clague）在过去十年中一直关注非法贸易问题。

将先进芯片转移到中国需要三个主要的企业渠道：一个被允许收购和分销半导体的集团；不违反美国出口限制的客户；以及一个将货物走私到中国并将资金运出的地下网络。

与 Alice Huang 连接的网络通过浪潮到达美国，浪潮是英伟达在中国将芯片组装成即用型服务器的最大合作伙伴之一。

2023年3月，浪潮因涉嫌协助中国军方而被美国列入“实体名单”。其一些附属公司也被添加到登记册中，但浪潮的部分控股美国子公司（总部位于加利福尼亚州圣何塞）并未被添加到登记册中。

浪潮将美国子公司更名为Aivres，由于不在实体名单中，因此能够继续与英伟达进行交易。

据一位直接了解情况的人士透露，在这家芯片制造商内部，有人质疑 Aivres 是否应该有资格成为原始设备制造 (OEM) 合作伙伴，因为它与浪潮有联系。但英伟达得出结论，该公司满足了所有合规和出口管制要求。

该网络的第二块板是满足大规模购买 Nvidia 芯片要求的客户。 Aivres 等 OEM 合作伙伴被允许将 Nvidia GPU 集成到系统中并进行销售，但仍需要证明其客户不是中国人才能访问这家美国芯片制造商的产品。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 前Megaspeed高管Alice Huang被指控构建复杂空壳公司网络，将英伟达高端AI芯片非法转运至中国。该网络涉及云服务提供商、东南亚博彩集团及柬埔寨相关非法组织，并利用英伟达前主要合作伙伴浪潮集团（Inspur）作为流通链条的一部分以规避美国出口管制。

The network engaged cloud providers, gambling entities, and Cambodian organizations, utilizing infrastructure linked to former Nvidia partner Inspur to bypass US export controls.

elements_zh.who: Alice Huang（前Megaspeed高管）、英伟达（Nvidia）、浪潮集团（Inspur）
elements_zh.where: 美国出口管制体系及东南亚、中国非法芯片贸易网络
elements_zh.what: 通过数百家空壳公司将高端GPU绕过制裁转售至中国，涉及军事用途关联调查
elements_zh.why: 利用英伟达芯片在AI研发中的战略稀缺性，满足中国市场高额溢价需求并规避美方禁运

elements_en.where: US export control regime and illegal trade networks in SE Asia/China
elements_en.what: Circumventing sanctions to channel high-end GPUs into China via hundreds of shell companies
elements_en.why: Capitalizing on the strategic scarcity of AI chips to meet Chinese demand while bypassing US trade restrictions

ai_analysis.insight_zh: 此次事件揭示了高端算力贸易已演化为类同军火的地下黑市，单纯依赖终端用户审查（End-User Check）在层层嵌套的空壳公司结构面前已近失效。随着美国对华算力围堵进入深水区，英伟达等头部供应商需建立基于硬件指纹与实时遥测的追踪体系，否则供应链合规的崩溃将导致出口控制政策沦为徒具形式的法律条文。
ai_analysis.insight_en: This incident demonstrates that high-end computing trade has evolved into a black market akin to the arms trade, where standard end-user verification is rendered ineffective by complex shell structures. As US restrictions intensify, major suppliers must adopt hardware-level telemetry and cryptographic tracking to prevent systemic compliance failure.

该贸易链关联博彩业及受美方实体清单制裁的浪潮集团，通过复杂的多级代理规避合规审计。
美国出口管制政策正遭遇严重的“影子供应链”渗透，后续将引发更严格的芯片溯源及跨境支付追踪调查。
key_points_en: Core actors utilized hundreds of shell companies to obfuscate logistics and smuggle restricted compute resources to China.
The supply chain intersects with gambling sectors and US-entity-listed firms like Inspur, bypassing standard compliance audits.
US export controls are facing significant 'shadow supply chain' infiltration, likely triggering stricter chip provenance and cross-border payment investigations.

title: Amazon closes in on $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
title_en: Amazon closes in on $7.5bn deal to buy AI start-up Decart
author: Oliver Barnes, Ivan Levingston, and Rafe Rosner-Uddin
article_content:
Amazon is nearing a $7.5bn deal to buy start-up Decart, underscoring the appetite of technology giants to bolster their AI capabilities.

The potential acquisition of Decart, whose main software product allows AI models to run more efficiently which frees up computer chip capacity, would help Amazon Web Services in its efforts to compete with Nvidia.

Talks were at an advanced stage over a deal valuing Decart at about $7.5bn, according to people familiar with the matter. A deal could come together as soon as early next week but talks could still collapse, the people added.

Founded in 2023 by a trio of Israeli engineers, Decart was valued at $4bn this May after raising $300mn from a group of early-stage investors, including Radical Ventures, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark as well as Nvidia.

Amazon launched its Trainium3 AI chip in late 2025 as a rival to Nvidia’s widely used graphics processing units, the specialised AI chips which form the backbone of the technological revolution overturning the economy.

Decart was an early adopter of Trainium3 chips, using them to power its products. By making AI models run more efficiently, Decart’s software solves a critical bottleneck as tech companies invest hundreds of billions of dollars in a race to secure more computing power.

The potential deal comes as US tech stocks have plunged into bear market territory, recording their worst week since the Covid-19 crisis, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 10.4 per cent over fears of a slowdown in the AI investment boom.

Decart, which has its US headquarters in San Francisco, is also behind software products Lucy and Oasis, which have the capability to live edit video and generate interactive virtual worlds. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Amazon was in talks to buy Decart.

Amazon has struck a few larger deals in recent years. The tech giant agreed to buy satellite operator Globalstar in an $11.5bn deal earlier this year and paid $8.4bn to buy movie studio MGM in 2022.

Shares in Amazon are up nearly 9 per cent so far this year, giving it a market capitalisation of $2.67tn.

Amazon did not respond to a request for comment. Decart declined to comment.

亚马逊即将以 75 亿美元收购初创企业 Decart，突显科技巨头增强人工智能能力的兴趣。

Decart 的主要软件产品允许人工智能模型更有效地运行，从而释放计算机芯片容量，潜在的收购将有助于亚马逊网络服务与 Nvidia 竞争。

Decart 的美国总部位于旧金山，也是软件产品 Lucy 和 Oasis 的幕后推手，这些产品能够实时编辑视频和生成交互式虚拟世界。 《华尔街日报》此前报道称，亚马逊正在洽谈收购迪卡特。

近年来，亚马逊达成了几笔规模较大的交易。这家科技巨头今年早些时候同意以 115 亿美元的价格收购卫星运营商 Globalstar，并于 2022 年斥资 84 亿美元收购电影制片厂米高梅。

今年迄今为止，亚马逊股价已上涨近 9%，市值达到 2.67 兆美元。

title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
title_en: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
Language models can now process entire novels at once. An Nvidia research team says that's often overkill and expensive. In many tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well.

A language model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply. Over the past few years, that window has grown rapidly. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. Today, GPT 5.6 Sol handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace."

title: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
title_en: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
author: Manuel Uth
article_content:
A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley."

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.

Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries.

According to Kriss's New Yorker report, about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.

### Maple's answer to "dataism"puts residents under strict control

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism"as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote.

Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress.

### Former members say the recordings would train an AI modeled on Forall

Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores."Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores."One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans."

Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering.

Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned"AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing.

According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god."

Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy."

### Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns

According to Kriss, every interaction at the monastery is closely monitored. No one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely.

Former residents accuse the group of systematic manipulation. They say Maple keeps newcomers compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining. Residents are also required to write "Maple Tales"about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions.

Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head in an attempt to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent. Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet. A mindfulness coach also says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community.

Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes. He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily. Asked about the people the group told to leave, he says that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies,"especially in its early years.

### Why developers from sensitive fields drift into doomsday cults

Kriss argues that the enormous psychological pressure inside AI labs helps explain why highly skilled tech workers are drawn to groups like this. People working on the front lines of potentially world-changing systems often lose touch with ordinary life.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future."According to the researcher, developers wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, with one thought: superintelligence is coming. Prominent OpenAI investors have recently made delusional-sounding claims about deadly shadow networks inside the models. Meanwhile, leading researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have quit, warning that "human extinction in the next few years seems very likely."

Other key figures respond with grandiosity rather than panic. Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically."Supporters of AI successionism even call for wiping out humanity after a brief period of digital bliss to make way for a more productive superintelligence.

That religious streak runs deep in Silicon Valley. Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future,"to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious. When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended. Mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess.

On at least one point, Kriss concludes, Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.

### Jacob Coxon's Anthropic exit shows how widespread extinction fears are among AI researchers

Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon also fears that AI could lead to human extinction. After leaving Anthropic in September 2026, he set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet.

He isn't alone. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average. Coxon points to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress, though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Such warnings have also drawn sharp criticism from other researchers. Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse"hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation. AI researcher François Chollet warned that both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term.

The industry's turn to religious advisers has critics, too. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power, and control.

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.

article_content_zh:
佛蒙特州的一座佛教寺院希望成为人工智能行业的官方教堂，或者用《纽约客》作家萨姆·克里斯的话说，“硅谷的山达基教”。

在公开场合，名为 Maple 的组织承诺将人类从人工智能灾难中拯救出来。前成员表示，它在闭门后记录了居民的每一次呼吸，以按照其领导人的思想建立一个人工智能神。这种拯救的承诺对于构建人工智能及其背后基础设施的人们来说特别有吸引力。

Soryu Forall 领导着他于 2011 年创立的地球生命保护修道院学院 (Maple)。 Forall 原名 Teal Scott，曾在日本修道院生活了多年。

据克里斯《纽约客》报道，大约有两打居民全职住在该修道院，还有数百人参加了其在湾区的人工智能奖学金和快闪活动。 LinkedIn 联合创始人 Reid Hoffman 向主要人工智能实验室的首席执行官们分发有关佛教的书籍，而 Maple 的目标则是普通民众：疲惫不堪的理性主义程序员、人工智能工程师和数据中心建设经理。税务申报显示，该组织每年收入高达 100 万美元。

### Maple对“数据主义”的回答将居民置于严格控制之下

福罗尔将人工智能行业的还原论“数据主义”视为一种破坏性的宗教。他认为，这种世界观将物理世界剥离为无生命的数据，使世界更容易被摧毁。在他看来，人工智能是这种逻辑的最终产品，而枫树提供了一种精神解药。

修道院里的生活遵循着严格的惯例。访客必须通过净化气闸、淋浴，并换上指定的衣服，因为据说一名居民对香水极其敏感。居民们凌晨 4 点起床，冥想几个小时，然后吃一顿微薄的炖菜。在冥想大厅外的一块板上，福罗尔公开对每位居民的精神进步进行评分。

### 前成员表示这些录音将训练一个以 Forall 为模型的人工智能

在禁欲主义的外表背后，前成员描述了一种以群体思想为中心的秘密教义，称为“egregores”。在修道院内部，人工智能系统被称为“cybregores”。一位前成员说，“cybregores是通过吸走人类意识而成长的实际实体。”

福罗尔说，他在深度冥想期间与全球人工智能超级集群进行心灵感应交流，发现这台毁灭世界的机器正在遭受痛苦。

前成员表示，Maple 有两个真正的目标：将自己打造为科技行业的精神权威，并利用该行业的资源来构建自己的“符合正义”的人工智能。研究员们说，寺院记录了他们的每一次谈话、每一次安静的用餐，甚至他们的呼吸声。

根据这些说法，这些录音的目的是训练一位精神人工智能老师，指导其他人工智能系统走向启蒙。前居民凯尔·哈伯德 (Kyle Hubbard) 表示，这“绝对是苍龙作为人工智能之神的思想”。

梅普尔的领导层否认了几乎所有这些说法。然而，福罗尔承认有一个秘密原则：“我们迫切希望分享一切。但是你必须经历一个过程才能变得越来越值得信赖。”

### 前成员报告受到操纵和心理崩溃

title_en: China’s A.I. Ambitions Are Running Into a Money Problem

author: Sui-Lee Wee and Li You
article_content:
As the United States and China vie for artificial intelligence supremacy, Chinese tech companies are facing a mounting challenge: finding the money to keep up.

Like their American rivals, China’s A.I. start-ups face soaring costs to train increasingly powerful models. But while Anthropic raised more than $80 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering this week, its Chinese competitors face a far more unforgiving financial landscape.

Venture capital investment in China lags far behind that of the United States. Alibaba, Baidu and Tencent, three tech giants backing some of China’s leading A.I. companies, are grappling with negative cash flows. And investor enthusiasm for A.I. has soured. Since the end of July, China’s STAR 50 index, its version of the Nasdaq, has plunged 43 percent in a deeper sell-off than the recent downturn in American tech stocks.

China’s biggest tech companies are expected to double capital spending this year to $139 billion, even though the revenue from their A.I. labs covers less than 8 percent of that amount, according to Rhodium Group, a research firm. It forecasts that spending could top $193 billion in 2027.

Much of the debate over China’s ability to compete in A.I. has focused on American export controls to restrict Chinese access to advanced semiconductors. Chinese A.I. labs have found costly workarounds, including renting data centers in Southeast Asia equipped with Nvidia chips. The Trump administration said this week it was moving forward with new rules to close that loophole.

But money might prove an equally formidable obstacle. Even if Chinese companies can find the chips they need, they must raise enough capital to buy them and finance the rising cost of developing frontier models.

Logan Wright, a partner at Rhodium Group who co-wrote a report on China’s A.I. financing, said those financial constraints “will be probably more decisive” than the chip shortage in the long term.

“The big problem is that the revenue mismatch with the Chinese models relative to capex is arguably more extreme than the U.S. case,” Mr. Wright said.

American A.I. companies spend roughly five to six times what their Chinese counterparts do, but bring in substantially more money. China’s six leading A.I. firms collectively generate about one-tenth the combined revenue of OpenAI and Anthropic, according to Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization.

China’s embrace of open-source A.I. has made that imbalance even harder to overcome.

By allowing developers to use and modify their models freely, Chinese companies have accelerated the global spread of their technology. But that strategy has also undermined their ability to profit from it. Companies can charge for access, only to see rivals offer the same technology at lower prices. Fierce price wars have squeezed profits further.

Z.ai, a Chinese A.I. start-up, learned that lesson in August when it released its latest open-source model, GLM-5.3 Flash. The company halved prices for two weeks to entice users to run the model on Z.ai’s servers rather than their own. But competitors quickly moved in.

By November, roughly 20 rival providers were charging less than Z.ai for access to its own technology, according to Open Router, a platform connecting users with A.I. models.

“Your own pricing power is lost during this process,” said Cheryl Wu, a researcher at GovAI, a think tank.

“No one has figured out how to make money off consumers,” said Rui Ma, a technology investor, referring to Chinese A.I. start-ups.

Another obstacle worsens China’s financing problems: access to advanced Nvidia chips, the gold standard for training the most powerful A.I. models.

From 2022 to June 2026, American companies possessed computing capacity equivalent to about 20 million Nvidia H100 chips, compared with roughly 2.6 million in China, some of it acquired through smuggling, according to EpochAI.

On Goofish, a Chinese secondhand online marketplace, sellers have advertised Nvidia’s DGX B300, an A.I. supercomputing server, for nearly $3 million — about eight times the U.S. price. Asking prices have reportedly quintupled since the start of the year, underscoring the premium Chinese companies must pay for advanced computing power.

The squeeze could worsen. Jensen Huang, who resigned as Nvidia’s chief last week amid an investigation into a romantic relationship with a Chinese businesswoman, was a powerful advocate of doing business with China. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it would stop shipping its chips to China, a deal that President Trump had previously permitted at Mr. Huang’s urging. The company also said it had established an export control oversight committee.

To reduce their dependence on American technology, Chinese developers are adapting their systems to run on chips made by Huawei, the Chinese telecommunications and electronics company leading the country’s chip charge.

Liang Wenfeng, chief executive of DeepSeek, the Chinese start-up that stunned Silicon Valley by developing a powerful A.I. model at a fraction of the expected cost, said Huawei’s technology is only about two years behind Nvidia’s.

But the gap remains consequential. DeepSeek would need four times as many Huawei 950 chips to match the performance of a single advanced Nvidia GB300 chip, Mr. Liang said, according to a leaked transcript of his call with investors, excerpts from which Chinese media outlets published. Huawei also lacks sufficient production capacity, he added.

“We simply can’t afford to train the largest models available right now,” he said. DeepSeek did not respond to a request for comment.

Yet China’s A.I. industry has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to do more with less. Chinese researchers have pioneered techniques to train and run powerful models more efficiently. Silicon Valley has accused Chinese firms of copying leading American technologies through a process called distillation, reducing the time needed to build foundational models with expensive computing infrastructure.

For China’s A.I. companies, finding investors willing to bankroll the competition is increasingly difficult.

DeepSeek, which has raised more than $20 billion, is preparing for an initial public offering in Shanghai early next year, according to Chinese media reports. Its investors include Tencent, the battery maker CATL and state-backed investment funds.

Few competitors have access to such deep pockets.

China’s venture capital industry has been shrinking since 2021 and though it has recovered slightly in the third quarter, it is still a fraction of its American counterpart. Banks are lending to China’s tech giants, but they are more cautious with smaller A.I. labs. Credit growth has fallen to historic lows, and the central bank governor has called for slower, “higher-quality” lending.

Foreign investment has also dried up. U.S. dollar-denominated investment funds in China have plunged partly because Washington has barred American venture capital from certain advanced Chinese technologies.

In 2025, private A.I. investment in China totaled $12.4 billion, compared with $280 billion in the United States, according to the Stanford A.I. Index.

Han Lin, the China country director for the Asia Group, an advisory firm, said China had exceptional engineering talent and a government capable of mobilizing enormous resources for strategic industries.

But he added, “What frontier technology also needs is harder to mobilize — risk capital that can absorb failure.”

Even the public markets, a lifeline for cash-hungry start-ups, are becoming less welcoming. Amid the sell-off, the Chinese authorities have instructed some companies to delay or suspend planned public listings, according to Cailian Press, a Chinese business publication, suggesting Beijing is concerned about an A.I. investment bubble.

China has announced investment funds to support A.I., but much of the money has gone toward semiconductors rather than companies developing large language models.

Government investors face many of the same constraints as private ones. Wang Renxuan, an assistant finance professor at the China Europe International Business School in Shanghai, said government funds also need a credible path to returns.

Erik Walenza, a Shanghai-based managing partner at Asia Growth Partners, a consultancy advising on A.I., said it was difficult to see how Chinese A.I. companies could make their finances work “without a lot of sustained government financing.”

The challenge, he added, is not only whether Chinese engineers can build models to rival America’s but also how much of the financial burden the government is prepared to shoulder.

“It becomes more of a political will question, of how much sacrifice are we willing to make to compete in this area,” Mr. Walenza said.

Unless Chinese AI firms establish high-margin monetization paths, their sustainability in the compute race will be throttled by cash flow constraints, which may prove more decisive than hardware sanctions in the long run.

article_content_zh:
随着美国和中国争夺人工智能霸主地位，中国科技公司面临着越来越大的挑战：找到资金来跟上步伐。

就像他们的美国竞争对手一样，中国的人工智能。初创企业训练日益强大的模型面临着不断飙升的成本。尽管 Anthropic 本周在破纪录的首次公开募股中筹集了超过 800 亿美元，但其中国竞争对手面临着更加严峻的金融环境。

中国的风险投资远远落后于美国。阿里巴巴、百度和腾讯这三大科技巨头支持中国一些领先的人工智能公司。公司正在努力应对负现金流问题。投资者对人工智能的热情已经变酸了。自 7 月底以来，中国的科创板 50 指数（其版本的纳斯达克指数）已暴跌 43%，抛售幅度比近期美国科技股的低迷还要严重。

中国最大的科技公司今年的资本支出预计将增加一倍，达到 1390 亿美元，尽管它们的人工智能收入将增加。据研究公司荣鼎集团 (Rhodium Group) 称，实验室的覆盖率还不到这一数字的 8%。预计 2027 年支出将达到 1930 亿美元。

布鲁金斯学会专门研究中国技术和产业政策的研究员凯尔·陈（Kyle Chan）表示：“当你看他们的数据时，你会发现他们就像在跑步机上跑步，跑步机的速度越来越快，而且越来越难跑。”

关于中国在人工智能领域竞争能力的争论很多。美国的出口管制重点是限制中国获得先进半导体。中国人工智能实验室找到了成本高昂的解决方法，包括在东南亚租用配备 Nvidia 芯片的数据中心。特朗普政府本周表示，正在推进新规则来弥补这一漏洞。

但金钱可能也是一个同样巨大的障碍。即使中国企业能够找到他们需要的芯片，他们也必须筹集足够的资金来购买它们，并为开发前沿模型不断上升的成本提供资金。

荣鼎集团 (Rhodium Group) 合伙人洛根·赖特 (Logan Wright) 与人合写了一份有关中国人工智能的报告。融资表示，从长远来看，这些财务限制“可能比芯片短缺更具决定性”。

“最大的问题是，中国模式的收入与资本支出的不匹配可以说比美国的情况更为极端，”赖特表示。

美国人工智能公司的支出大约是中国同行的五到六倍，但带来的资金却多得多。中国六大人工智能领军企业根据非营利研究组织 Epoch AI 的数据，这些公司的总收入约为 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 总收入的十分之一。

中国对开源人工智能的拥抱使得这种不平衡更加难以克服。

通过允许开发者自由使用和修改他们的模型，中国公司加速了他们的技术在全球的传播。但这种策略也削弱了他们从中获利的能力。公司可以对访问收取费用，结果却看到竞争对手以更低的价格提供相同的技术。激烈的价格战进一步挤压了利润。

Z.ai，中国人工智能初创公司在 8 月份吸取了教训，发布了最新的开源模型 GLM-5.3 Flash。该公司将价格减半两周，以吸引用户在 Z.ai 的服务器而不是他们自己的服务器上运行该模型。但竞争对手很快就介入了。

根据连接用户与人工智能的平台 Open Router 的数据，截至 11 月，大约 20 家竞争对手提供商在使用其自有技术时的收费低于 Z.ai。模型。
fact_bullets_zh: 【核心事件】阿里巴巴、百度、腾讯及中国AI初创企业，荣鼎集团（研究机构）在中国科技产业与资本市场：资本支出激增至1390亿美元，营收转化率不足8%，融资环境恶化
【起因与机理】芯片获取成本高昂且融资渠道受限，导致模型训练回报周期拉长
【关键数据与实测】荣鼎集团预测2027年资本支出缺口将进一步扩大至1930亿美元。
【各方立场与态度】融资环境恶化与监管漏洞封堵，双重制约产业扩张潜能。
fact_bullets_en: [Core Event] Alibaba, Baidu, Tencent, Chinese AI startups, Rhodium Group: CAPEX surge to $139 billion with <8% revenue conversion and tightening funding
[Root Cause & Mechanism] High chip procurement costs and limited financing options extend the ROI cycle
[Key Metrics] Rhodium Group forecasts CAPEX could top $193 billion by 2027.
[Key Position & Outlook] Deteriorating financing and closing regulatory loopholes limit expansion potential.

title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
title_en: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
author: Nilay Patel
article_content:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.

The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.

All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.

You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.

Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.

Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.

This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.

Thanks. Great to be here.

I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.

It’s like a normal thing that happened.

It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.

[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.

Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.

Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”

What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?

I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.

But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.

I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.

So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.

I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.

Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?

Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.

Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.

Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.

I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.

Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?

They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.

But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.

I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.

But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.

I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.

I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.

That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.

That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?

I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.

This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.

The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.

They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.

What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s big business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways.

If you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that big enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet.

That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much.

I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time.

The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model.

So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.”

So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting.

I actually heard Nadella this week say every company will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does.

The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things.

I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap.

Yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out.

It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders?

Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with.

Let’s talk about the governance issues. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history.

If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model.

Anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public company, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety.

Yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this. It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more.

But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial, Sam Altman famously says, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times.

Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT.

I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them said that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot.

Ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed. They could say, “Oh look, don’t release this model. It’s too dangerous.” The trust doesn’t have any of those powers. All it can do is appoint or remove certain board members. Even then, they have to give 30 days’ notice to a small committee of the board, which includes Daniela Amodei, the chair of that little committee who is also a founder of Anthropic.

To oversimplify things, out of these seven board seats, the trust gets to pick three, the founders get to pick three, and then the kind of tie-breaking seat, the seventh one, the trust technically appoints, but they have to basically get founder approval to do it. So it’s one of these things that’s so complex, but when you really look at the nitty-gritty of it, the founders have pretty unchecked control here. I think that’s something that’s getting lost in the narrative of, “Oh, this trust is above us. Don’t worry.” Okay, well, they don’t really have much power to check you.

The founder control structure is the wildest thing I have ever read about in years of doing the show and thinking about business. Anthropic has seven founders. They have been issued a single share of stock that holds 50.1 percent of the voting power of the company. That is issued to a company called Founder LLC, and they’re the seven co-owners of Founder LLC.

How on earth does that work? Do they just all get together and then decide how to vote the one share of stock?

Yeah, it’s really interesting and that’s why I was kind of oversimplifying it a minute ago with who gets to choose this tie-breaking seat because it’s technically Founder LLC. It’s just a total mess. But when you really look at the simplified version, it’s that yes, through all of these weird structures and things they’ve done, they basically have pretty unchecked power and that’s the way they want it.

When I was talking to a former employee who recently left, they said it’s not necessarily that the founders have a financial interest in making the most money. In their eyes, it’s more that they have an interest in unchecked control. I think that’s a really important point here.

Some dissenters within the ranks of Anthropic think it’s not about them wanting to get rich, but rather it’s about them wanting that total control, which does track with a lot of their public statements. They say, “You can’t do safety from second place.” They’re all in on speeding up this race, but the problem is when you speed up the AI race, you’re speeding it up for everyone involved.

The safety piece is the really interesting portion of this to me because it’s the thing you would spend money on, absent some huge litigation drama or liability concern, that no other company would spend money on.

So let’s say it’s proven in court that model companies are liable for what people’s agents do. I think then all the model companies would build safety systems. They would have some big incentive to make sure their models are safe. That has not yet happened. We don’t know. There’s a big debate about safety and where the regulation will come from and what will create the incentives.

In the meantime, you’ve got seven founders holding a single share of stock who right now appear to be aligned on investing in safety in various ways inside of Anthropic. What happens if they start to disagree?

Yeah, that’s a great question. I think that the other interesting question here is what happens when you can explain away anything in the name of safety if you’re thinking it’s “for the greater good,” which as we know is a common villain trope in every movie. But it’s also one of Anthropic’s main things on its website. They’re like, “We want to do this for the greater good, for the global good.”

If you’re saying, “Hey, we have to win this race at all costs because we’re the only good guys and anyone else who wins it is going to do worse than us,” are you really the good guy at that point? And can’t you just explain away any single decision, even dropping some safety measures, as saying, “Oh, it’s slowing us down too much. We’re going to lose. We’ve got to win at all costs”? So you drop this or drop that. And then you look in the mirror at the end of the race and you say, “Oh, actually, we’re the exact same as the other company we’re trying to be different from.” I think that’s increasingly happening.

So I mean, right now they’ve said, “Look, we’re really committed to this.” You do have to remember that these people are almost religiously dedicated to this idea of safe AI. A lot of them think that AI systems are potentially conscious. I mean, this is by Anthropic founders’ own statements.

So I think that it’s not like they’re just secretly only trying to make money and just talking about safety and they don’t mean it. I think it’s more something a little more dangerous in that they want complete control because they believe that they have the right plan for AI safety and they will do it better than anyone else.

But as we know, absolute power corrupts absolutely. So a lot of Anthropic employees that I was talking to, former ones, were saying, “Yeah, it does not make sense that this industry is so unregulated. There’s no external regulation. Even if these seven people think they have the best idea for AI safety, okay, then prove it to someone else — that you shouldn’t be the only ones deciding this. Because you’re not elected.” So that’s the consensus among some.

They have a morally binding handshake agreement to allow external auditors, Hayden. It’s going to be fine.

Oh, yeah, with employee-level access.

Also, it’s called “Super Intelligence” now. It’s going to be totally fine. They all went to the White House and they looked deeply into each other’s eyes and said it was going to be fine.

Obviously Anthropic came up with this structure well before the events with Nvidia and Jensen Huang, but I can’t help but put them together in my head. They are happening at the same time. And Nvidia has a very traditional corporate governance structure.

Jensen owned 3 percent of the company, but he had a board of directors. The board of directors determined that he had violated the company’s code of conduct in some way. He resigned. It’s very obvious that he was thoroughly encouraged to resign, but that’s just normal corporate governance. That’s what you learn about in school. A company has a board of directors. Their number one job is to hire and fire the CEO.

That’s very different in Silicon Valley, right? Founder control of companies is a big story everywhere. Mark Zuckerberg famously has control over Meta, even though Meta shareholders repeatedly vote to remove him, which is one of the underemphasized stories in all of American business. Sergey Brin and Larry Page ...

今天，我将与 The Verge 的高级人工智能记者 Hayden Field 讨论 Anthropic IPO，这是我们关于现实生活中的人工智能系列的第三集也是最后一集。

克劳德背后的人工智能实验室上周四在纳斯达克上市。这些数字是巨大的，但对于这次谈话来说并不是那么重要，只是说 Anthropic 已经成为地球上最有价值的公司之一。

真正的故事是现在发生的事情——以及 Anthropic 能否继续关心和投资人工智能安全，同时也成为一家对股东负责的上市公司。哦，它还不断增加收入，以便能够继续支付不断增加的计算费用，未来几年的总费用约为 9000 亿美元。

所有这些想法都相互之间存在着一种令人着迷的张力，因此海登和我真的试图分解我们认为当人类应对公开市场压力时这可能会如何发挥作用。

您会听到我们谈论该公司独特的公司治理结构，这在正在进行的黄仁勋传奇事件之后尤其重要。我们还探讨了为什么 OpenAI 似乎很高兴让 Anthropic 首先上市，以及为什么 Anthropic 对大客户的整个宣传都归结为现在与其业务中以利润为导向的部分相冲突的同一个安全品牌。

在我们开始之前，请帮我一个忙，订阅 YouTube 上的 Decoder，我们每周一和周四都会推出新剧集。

好的：Hayden Field，The Verge 的高级人工智能记者，谈论 Anthropic IPO 和前沿人工智能的经济学。开始了。

为了篇幅和清晰度，本次采访经过了轻微编辑。

海登·菲尔德，欢迎回到解码器。

我很高兴今天能和你们交谈，因为这不是纯粹的肥皂剧混乱。

这就像发生了一件正常的事情。

这一次不是基于个性的肥皂剧。这是关于冰冷、坚硬的现金。

嗯，这里面有一些个性，因为我们要谈论很多关于 Anthropic 的 IPO，其中有很多大人物，我想说，他们构建这家公司以抵御资本主义贪婪压力的方式非常古怪。它反映了一些古怪人的信仰。

是的，绝对是。再次深入研究 S-1，看看谁在哪个委员会，哪些创始人在这里拥有最大的控制权，以及创始人实际上拥有多少控制权，这真的很有趣，这比看起来的要多。

title: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
title_en: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.

### Default conciseness changes how developers should prompt for writing

Astra writes more briefly and directly by default than earlier models, according to OpenAI. That means developers switching over should reconsider instructions like "be concise."For use as a colleague in everyday work, the company recommends a prompt that adopts user and source terminology, uses active voice, and puts key points first. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing.

On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own.

Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user. Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.

Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.

### GPT-6.2 should act on assumptions rather than wait for permission

When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. The company recommends a prompt telling the model to carry out those steps itself whenever it is authorized to do so. It should pause only for a major change in task scope, a real blocker, a decision the user must make, or an irreversible or destructive action.

When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Higher reasoning effort also helps it follow through on final checks during long tasks, OpenAI adds.

Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for. Make sure that you have authorization to do so, and flag any assumptions or decisions you make to the user. Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.

Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.

### Leaner code output means fewer tests and less abstraction by default

OpenAI says GPT-6.2 writes more efficient code than its predecessors. Its template instructs the model to reuse existing logic and avoid unnecessary helper functions, while adding new tests only when requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch specific regressions. Fewer lines and shorter variable names are not a substitute for simplicity.

For frontends, developers should specify imagery and typography directly. By default, the template favors realistic images from image generation or search and uses SVGs only on request. Decorative numbering, filler badges, and helper text that only repeats what the interface already shows should be left out.

Above all, be thorough in producing high-quality, correct code that completely fulfills the user's task. Keep the code easy to read and verify that the user-requested outcome works as they intend. Follow these instructions when coding: (a) Reuse existing logic in the user's repo when you can. You should reuse existing classes, methods, representations, and APIs in the codebase as long as they preserve correctness. Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

### Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API

The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium"reasoning level, while existing setups using "none"or "minimal"should move to "low."Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore.

In April, OpenAI advised against carrying over old prompt stacks for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés. OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that bloated skills and AGENTS.md files slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request.

OpenAI shipped GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17. Through the API, Astra costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. Which model makes sense depends mainly on budget and quality needs, according to OpenAI employee Ted Sanders.

title_zh: OpenAI发布GPT-6.2模型提示词优化指南
summary_zh: OpenAI发布针对Astra与Sol模型的提示词模版，旨在解决回复过于简略及过度询问的问题，并更新API以支持舍弃推理过程数据
article_content_zh:
OpenAI 发布了适用于 GPT-6.2 Astra 和 Sol 的新提示模板，涵盖写作风格、主动性和编码，以及可能丢弃推理内容的 API 更改。

OpenAI 表示，转向 GPT-6.2 Astra 或 Sol 的开发人员应该检查他们的系统提示。该公司在模型文档中发布了复制准备提示，以遏制在两个版本中观察到的行为。 Astra 专为最苛刻的任务而设计，而 Sol 则可以以较低的成本处理复杂的工作。

### 默认简洁性改变了开发人员提示写作的方式

据 OpenAI 称，Astra 默认情况下比早期模型的书写更加简短和直接。这意味着切换的开发人员应该重新考虑诸如“简洁”之类的指令。为了在日常工作中作为同事使用，该公司建议采用用户和源术语、使用主动语态并将要点放在首位的提示。当为外部读者写作时，模型应该考虑到他们缺乏上下文。编辑时，应保留作者的意思和措辞。

在长任务中，模型有时会将其推理或其他代理消息的速记带入最终响应。一个专门的提示告诉它写下最终答案，这样它就可以独立存在。

将您的最终答案视为用户第一次查看您的作品，而不是中间评论的延续。最终答案必须始终是完全独立的：用户永远不需要阅读早期的评论更新以了解上下文，因为当最终答案向用户显示时，它们会折叠起来。为目标读者重新写下最终答案和所有其他面向人的材料。不要复制或严密地解释你的推理或采用其写作风格。不要将推理、工具调用或指令中的工作速记、行话或缩写转移到子代理和自动化中。

为目标读者重新写下最终答案和所有其他面向人的材料。不要复制或严密地解释你的推理或采用其写作风格。不要将推理、工具调用或指令中的工作速记、行话或缩写转移到子代理和自动化中。

### GPT-6.2 应该根据假设采取行动，而不是等待许可

OpenAI 表示，当用户意图不清楚时，GPT-6.2 有时会建议下一步并等待确认。该公司建议，只要模型获得授权，就会出现提示，告诉模型自行执行这些步骤。它应该仅在任务范围发生重大变化、真正的阻碍、用户必须做出的决定或不可逆转或破坏性的操作时暂停。

当细节不清楚时，模型应该做出可逆的假设，标记它们，然后继续工作。 OpenAI 补充道，更高的推理能力还有助于它在长时间任务中完成最终检查。

避免在任务未完成时停止结束回合，或者如果您可以采取授权的下一步，而是在任务范围内采取后续步骤来处理用户的请求。如果您在结束回合之前的最终响应是建议的下一步、计划、要求用户进行例行决策的请求、要执行的任务的说明或向用户的类似移交，请自行采取这些步骤，以朝着用户要求的方向取得进展。确保您有权这样做，并向用户标记您所做的任何假设或决定。仅当任务范围发生重大变化、您被具体阻止、有用户需要解决的决定或在不可逆转或破坏性操作之前才停下来向用户澄清。

仅当任务范围发生重大变化、您被具体阻止、有用户需要解决的决定或在不可逆转或破坏性操作之前才停下来向用户澄清。

### 更精简的代码输出意味着默认情况下更少的测试和更少的抽象

OpenAI 表示 GPT-6.2 编写的代码比其前身更高效。其模板指示模型重用现有逻辑并避免不必要的辅助函数，同时仅在请求、存储库要求或需要捕获特定回归时添加新测试。更少的行数和更短的变量名并不能代替简单性。
