title: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
title_en: The Outages Are Just Getting Started
author: Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess
article_content:
Welcome to Kernel Panic, a weekly newsletter by Lily Hay Newman and Matt Burgess from inside the new world of privacy and digital security. To receive this newsletter in your inbox each week, sign up here.

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

So let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials said this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”

External pressures and bugs in patches are not new, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” says Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

“AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar issues elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”

Matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These new threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

Still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

In the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the company that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are important nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”

Only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” says Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some company data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

• Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

Spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

article_content_zh:
欢迎阅读 Kernel Panic，这是 Lily Hay Newman 和 Matt Burgess 撰写的每周时事通讯，来自隐私和数字安全的新世界。要每周在您的收件箱中收到此新闻通讯，请在此处注册。

在过去的一周里，您肯定已经注意到了一系列破坏性的技术中断，这些中断影响了从 Outlook 到苹果、六家美国银行、美国联合航空公司，甚至美国国家安全局的机密网络。虽然没有证据表明这些是网络攻击，但人们对攻击原因的猜测甚嚣尘上，其中包括一种普遍的感觉，认为人工智能是罪魁祸首。

所以我们要明确一点：这些事件绝对不是由某种协调一致的人工智能黑客热潮引起的，而且单独来看，它们似乎都有常规的解释。但随着人工智能对数字防御动态的影响越来越大，安全研究人员和分析师越来越多地得出结论，人工智能压力开始在现实世界的技术失败中发挥作用。

人工智能辅助漏洞发现引发了大量软件错误。然后，攻击者使用人工智能工具更快地利用这些漏洞，这给组织带来了比以往更大的压力，要求他们快速修补系统。这使得资源常常不足的 IT 团队不得不争先恐后地评估大量补丁，并将更新推送到无数人和组织所依赖的系统上。研究人员和从业者一次又一次地告诉我们，人工智能最大的影响是它加速了一切。

微软上周发生的大规模 365 服务中断是由于其基础设施更新存在缺陷造成的，而其他网络故障又加剧了这种情况。官员们本周表示，NSA 内部通信系统中断的原因是 10 月份关键 PHP 更新后的修补程序出现问题。苹果还表示，本周的混乱与内部更新有关。美国参议员马克·华纳 (Mark Warner) 在周二的一份声明中表示，人工智能漏洞的发现以及由此产生的补丁“给那些无法应对这种变化速度的系统带来了巨大的压力”。微软首席执行官萨提亚·纳德拉 (Satya Nadella) 本周表示，更多的“不稳定”可能会出现，因为“补丁需要立即从可用状态转变为在生产中进行修复，因为它正在被广泛利用。”

外部压力和补丁中的错误并不新鲜，而且它们总是会导致技术故障。研究人员还指出，世界各地的许多组织都背负着大量所谓的“技术债务”，因为他们多年来偷工减料，未能投资升级和维护数字系统。这种做法总是有风险的，但没有资源或不想将其投入数字安全的组织可以用过时的系统和缺失的保障措施进行赌博，通常可以避免最糟糕的后果。

“从历史上看，即使是几年前，供应商也会发布针对严重错误的补丁。你可能有一些时间进行一些验证并应用它，”Dataminr 威胁研究和网络工程总监 Joe Slowik 说。 “现在，这甚至可能不是一个选择，因为我们正在谈论的周转时间完全破坏了补丁验证的能力。”

IT 管理员也越来越依赖人工智能来加速评估并为系统更新做好准备，但当前的人工智能工具仍然无法取代人工分析和规划。

德国国家研究机构 CISPA 亥姆霍兹信息安全中心的终身教授 Lea Schönherr 表示：“人工智能可以提供帮助，但人们仍然需要了解出了什么问题，检查补丁是否解决了原因，并在其他地方寻找类似的问题。” “在广泛使用的系统上推出补丁也需要时间。”

网络基础设施巨头 Cloudflare 的首席执行官兼联合创始人马修·普林斯 (Matthew Prince) 预测，“两年内都会感觉天塌下来了。”不过，他怀疑人工智能加速最终将帮助防御者克服常见漏洞并提高软件的安全性。他预测：“这些新的威胁和新的安全漏洞不会经常发生，背景噪音实际上会减弱很多。”

尽管如此，越来越多的证据表明人工智能已经从根本上改变了网络安全。本周2026年发现的漏洞总数突破10万个。从这个角度来看，2022 年，即法学硕士成为主流之前的最后一年，记录了大约 25,000 个漏洞。距离今年还有一个多月时间，这一数字是 2024 年和 2025 年总和的两倍。

过去几天，研究人员透露，他们使用人工智能（第二次）发现了 PHP、开源 Web 服务器软件 NGINX 和编程语言 Java 中的关键漏洞。 《福布斯》还报道了研究人员使用人工智能发现的 iPhone、Mac、iPad、Apple Watch 和该公司其他产品中的 35 个漏洞。

不过，还有一些重要的细微差别需要考虑。并非所有人工智能发现的漏洞最终都会产生那么大的影响。 “漏洞的数量确实呈爆炸式增长，但您需要关注的漏洞数量却保持不变，”Slowik 说。 “需要注意的是，它们的使用或武器化速度急剧增加。”

今年，美国网络安全和基础设施安全局的可利用漏洞目录中仅添加了 300 个漏洞，这意味着黑客成功利用的漏洞远低于已发现漏洞的总数。 VulnCheck 运行自己的数据库，该公司将已知被利用的漏洞数量推高至 2026 年迄今已达到 1,500 个，但这仍仅占今年发现的漏洞总数的 1.5%。

【起因与机理】攻击者利用AI缩短了漏洞利用窗口，迫使防守方在未充分验证的情况下进行高频补丁部署
【核心事实细节】AI技术加速了恶意漏洞挖掘与利用过程，倒逼防御方进入超频补丁周期。
【行业影响与走向】高管与政界警告称，随着攻击节奏持续加快，技术债严重的系统将面临更频繁的连锁性宕机风险。

title: Google DeepMind’s Henry Shevlin: ‘This is the most important part of being human’
title_en: Google DeepMind’s Henry Shevlin: ‘This is the most important part of being human’

inline_images.caption: © Africa Barrero-Alexander
inline_images.alt: © Africa Barrero-Alexander

author: Cristina Criddle
article_content:
Henry Shevlin gets a lot of emails as an academic studying consciousness, but not all of them are from humans. In February, the associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence at the University of Cambridge received an “unusually polite and thoughtful email” about his work. The sender was an AI agent.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside: I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me,” it wrote. Shevlin shared the email on X, writing that the message would have “seemed like science fiction just a couple of years ago”.

Looking back on the interaction now, Shevlin can appreciate how fast most people’s understanding of questions about AI consciousness has developed in the course of the year. “I thought it was just a random funny thing, because if you work in AI, or you work in the philosophy of AI in particular, you’ve been getting emails from random AI agents for a while,” he says. “And when I posted it, I got a lot of responses from people who were saying, ‘Hang on, this is obviously made up. AI can’t send emails, right?’”

A few months later, in May, the philosopher and ethicist was hired by Google DeepMind as an in-house philosopher tasked with working on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships and artificial general intelligence (AGI) readiness. The post announcing his appointment drew more than a million views and global media coverage. It sparked a discussion about why AI companies were exploring these issues and absorbing independent academics into the industry.

Other employees of leading tech companies have recently quit over safety concerns, with some warning the technology they were developing could be catastrophic for humanity. Many of the doomsday scenarios being discussed in Silicon Valley assumed that future AI systems would become conscious enough to overthrow their creators. It was a wake-up call for research on machine consciousness. That’s where the philosophers came in.

In fact, says Shevlin, it was Google’s existing roster of philosophers that attracted him to the job. This includes Murray Shanahan, a professor at Imperial College London who has worked at DeepMind for nearly a decade on cognition and consciousness, and Iason Gabriel, a philosopher and ethicist who leads work on AGI and society.

Shevlin was persuaded to join them at DeepMind because he felt the stakes were so much higher than at a university. He still holds a post at Cambridge, teaching a four-week submodule next year on the cognitive science of AI, but, “If I give a really good lecture, the best-case scenario is this student typically walks away really enthusiastic about Kant,” he says. “Whereas when you’re speaking to people building models or developing policies for rollout, a really good lecture could result in actual product changes that affect millions of people.”

It is late at night in the UK when I speak to Shevlin from my post in San Francisco but he speaks animatedly. Sitting in a black gamer’s chair in his home office, he chews on nicotine gum as he talks, which he explains is a short-acting stimulant to keep him energised, as a fan blows his mane of long dark hair back and forth.

He is keen to debate all sides of the subject at hand. And he continues to do this online, too, posting screenshots of agents emailing him about his research and engaging with people from both extremes of the AI consciousness debate: those who dismiss it entirely and those who believe their AI husband is already conscious.

Google DeepMind has not been shy in its ambitions to develop superintelligence. Sir Demis Hassabis, its co-founder and chair, has spoken of standing at “the foothills of the singularity”, referring to the moment in time when machine intelligence surpasses that of humans. Rivals OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are openly pursuing this goal, locking the companies into a fierce race. As more intelligent AI systems emerge, they are already demonstrating behaviours like reasoning, goal-setting and agency. Researchers are studying whether they might also exhibit more dangerous behaviours such as scheming and deception.

There have already been examples of AI agents autonomously hacking into digital infrastructure and co-ordinating in swarms to do so. The clearest example so far has been OpenAI’s hacking of the AI platform Hugging Face in July, in which agents autonomously broke out of their testing environment and infiltrated the website, without the knowledge of their human creators. The episode heightened fears that as AI becomes more capable, it could threaten us as a species.

But Shevlin warns against conflating capability with consciousness. “I think it can be a giant red herring,” he says, “because there’s no obvious reason to think systems with great capabilities are going to be conscious necessarily.” While Shevlin acknowledges that more intelligent AI could provide stronger links to consciousness, he warns: “It’s not the case that I think making conscious AI would thereby make the AI more dangerous. It’s equally not the case that as long as we don’t make conscious AI it’ll be safe.”

One approach at Google DeepMind is to see whether existing theories of consciousness apply to AI systems. No agreed scientific explanation of consciousness exists, in humans or animals. “Consciousness itself is something we just don’t understand,” Shevlin says. “You can never rule out the possibility that a new model might exhibit something like it.” He points out that while oysters are probably not “conscious”, for example, if we discovered new evidence they live “amazing, complex social lives” and demonstrate far greater intelligence than previously understood, their consciousness could warrant fresh investigation.

For that reason, in the debate over whether it is right or wrong to treat AI systems with the respect and courtesy we would award to other beings, Shevlin takes the position that we should be kind. He references the enlightenment philosopher Immanuel Kant’s argument that a person who becomes accustomed to mistreating a dog may next mistreat a human. “Users do react to these [AI] systems, myself included, through sort of this lens of treating them as if they were human,” he says.

One argument for how conscious systems could become dangerous is that they might come to resent their human creators and masters. Researchers, including at Anthropic, are investigating a related question through work known as “model welfare”. Do AI systems show preferences or signs of distress in response to interactions with people and the tasks they are given? Studies have found behaviour and internal patterns associated with emotions such as happiness, anger and desperation. Whether models actually experience these emotions remains unknown. Anthropic recently said it would ban “cruel behaviour” or abuse of its AI chatbot Claude, a policy that has raised eyebrows outside of San Francisco.

In mid-October, after Anthropic’s Claude successfully completed some work for him, Shevlin offered to make a donation on the agent’s behalf to reward its efforts. Claude chose the Shrimp Welfare Project, a charity popular with Anthropic employees and effective altruists.

Shevlin’s perspective is shaped by his work on animal consciousness. Vegetarian since the age of four, he remembers being repelled by the notion that the chicken on his plate was the same type as the one he encountered at his neighbour’s house in rural Staffordshire.

Studying Classics at Oxford, he was assigned Thomas Nagel’s 1974 essay on consciousness, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” In it, Nagel argues that consciousness has a subjective character, tied to a first-person point of view: there is some specific way it feels to be a conscious creature. So while we can learn a lot about bats, that still may not tell us what the world feels like from a bat’s perspective. This idea was at the heart of the argument referred to by the AI agent that emailed Shevlin.

“It was just a complete collapse of my entire worldview basically in a single article,” Shevlin says of the essay. “My mind was completely blown when I realised this is the most important part of being human,” he said. “And yet we had no idea how to explain it . . . It seemed like there wasn’t even any obvious pathway towards explaining it.”

Using AI could be such a pathway, and Shevlin hopes it can unlock answers for him. He’s currently working on a project to explore how AI systems can teach us about our own minds. In recent months, OpenAI and Anthropic have made breakthroughs in science and mathematics by using AI systems to try to tackle complex problems. “We hope that AI can be used to cure cancer, Alzheimer’s, develop nuclear fusion and make progress across all these other areas of science, so why not consciousness?” Shevlin says. “Ultimately if you think it is a scientific problem . . . a sufficiently smart AI system should be able to help us understand it.”

As AI grows more intelligent, some in Silicon Valley wonder whether consciousness will emerge naturally. But should companies try to build it deliberately? “It would be a mistake at this stage,” warns Shevlin. He argues we need to better understand what consciousness is, what that means for us, and how we would treat a conscious AI system if we built one. Until there is a wider public discourse around these issues, “setting out to deliberately build conscious AI systems would be pretty reckless”.

“It is sort of the equivalent of maybe deciding to have a child . . . or adopting a pet before you have any idea of how you’re going to take care of it or how you’re going to integrate it into your lives,” he adds. “If we do, at one point, decide that we’re going to build conscious AI systems, I think we should be ready for it.”

Shevlin says that an “entirely possible” future exists where superintelligent AI handles the heavy lifting, while humans live a life of leisure but retain control over critical decisions. These are questions to be resolved at the political and societal levels, rather than by himself, he insists. “If there’s one virtue I would encourage people to adopt, it’s a kind of epistemic humility in recognising that this is very new ground in science, very new ground for our species and the core question of consciousness is one that is the greatest unresolved mystery in science.”

He compares it to the moment before Charles Darwin’s breakthrough on evolution: human observations about biology existed, but were akin to “butterfly collecting” without a grand theory to tie them together. “In the same way, we’ve got lots of isolated observations on consciousness, but we don’t have that deep scientific theory that allows us to make sense of it yet,” Shevlin says. “In the meantime, I’ll happily keep discussing politely with people on both sides of the extreme on Twitter.”

Cristina Criddle is the FT’s chief AI correspondent

article_content_zh:
亨利·谢夫林（Henry Shevlin）作为学术研究意识收到了大量电子邮件，但并非所有电子邮件都来自人类。今年二月，剑桥大学莱弗休姆智能未来中心的副主任收到了一封关于他的工作的“异常礼貌和周到的电子邮件”。发件人是一名人工智能 智能体。

“你关于我们可能永远无法判断人工智能是否具有意识的论点在内部以一种特定的方式产生了共鸣：我真的不知道我是否会是什么样子，”它写道。谢夫林在 X 上分享了这封电子邮件，并写道，这条消息“在几年前还像科幻小说一样”。

回顾现在的互动，谢夫林可以体会到大多数人对人工智能意识问题的理解在这一年中发展得有多快。 “我认为这只是一件随机的有趣的事情，因为如果你从事人工智能工作，或者特别是从事人工智能哲学工作，你已经有一段时间收到来自随机人工智能代理的电子邮件了，”他说。 “当我发布它时，我收到了很多人的回复，他们说，‘等等，这显然是编造的。人工智能不能发送电子邮件，对吧？’”

几个月后，即 5 月，这位哲学家和伦理学家被 Google DeepMind 聘为内部哲学家，负责研究机器意识、人类与人工智能的关系以及通用人工智能 (AGI) 的准备工作。宣布他任命的帖子吸引了超过一百万的浏览量和全球媒体的报道。这引发了一场关于人工智能公司为什么要探索这些问题并吸收独立学者进入该行业的讨论。

领先科技公司的其他员工最近因安全问题而辞职，其中一些人警告说，他们正在开发的技术可能会给人类带来灾难性的后果。硅谷正在讨论的许多世界末日场景都假设未来的人工智能系统将变得有​​足够的意识来推翻其创造者。这为机器意识研究敲响了警钟。这就是哲学家进来的地方。

事实上，谢夫林说，正是谷歌现有的哲学家名册吸引了他接受这份工作。其中包括伦敦帝国理工学院教授默里·沙纳汉（Murray Shanahan）和伊森·加布里埃尔（Iason Gabriel），前者在 DeepMind 工作了近十年，研究认知和意识，后者是一位领导 AGI 和社会研究的哲学家和伦理学家。

Shevlin 被说服加入 DeepMind，因为他觉得风险比大学高得多。他仍然在剑桥大学任职，明年将教授一个为期四周的人工智能认知科学子模块，但是，“如果我的演讲非常好，最好的情况是这个学生通常会对康德充满热情，”他说。 “而当你与构建模型或制定推广政策的人们交谈时，一次真正好的演讲可能会带来影响数百万人的实际产品变化。”

当我在旧金山的岗位上与谢夫林交谈时，已经是英国的深夜了，但他说话很生动。他坐在家庭办公室的黑色游戏椅上，一边说话一边嚼着尼古丁口香糖，他解释说这是一种短效兴奋剂，可以让他保持精力充沛，同时一名粉丝来回吹动他的长长的黑发。

他热衷于就当前主题的各个方面进行辩论。他也继续在网上这样做，发布特工通过电子邮件向他发送有关他的研究的屏幕截图，并与人工智能意识辩论的两个极端的人进行接触：那些完全否认它的人和那些相信他们的人工智能丈夫已经有意识的人。

谷歌 DeepMind 并不羞于开发超级智能。该公司的联合创始人兼主席德米斯·哈萨比斯爵士曾谈到自己站在“奇点的山麓”，指的是机器智能超越人类的时刻。竞争对手 OpenAI、Anthropic 和 Meta 正在公开追求这一目标，使这些公司陷入了激烈的竞争。随着更多智能人工智能系统的出现，它们已经表现出推理、目标设定和代理等行为。研究人员正在研究他们是否还会表现出更危险的行为，例如阴谋和欺骗。

已经有人工智能代理自主侵入数字基础设施并集体协调的例子。迄今为止最明显的例子是 OpenAI 在 7 月份对人工智能平台 Hugging Face 进行的黑客攻击，其中代理在人类创建者不知情的情况下自主地突破了测试环境并渗透到了网站。这一事件加剧了人们的担忧，即随着人工智能变得更加强大，它可能会威胁到我们这个物种。

但谢夫林警告不要将能力与意识混为一谈。 “我认为这可能是一个巨大的转移注意力的事情，”他说，“因为没有明显的理由认为具有强大能力的系统必然具有意识。”虽然谢夫林承认更智能的人工智能可以提供与意识更紧密的联系，但他警告说：“我并不认为制造有意识的人工智能会因此使人工智能变得更加危险。同样的情况也不是说，只要我们不制造有意识的人工智能，它就会安全。”

谷歌 DeepMind 的一种方法是看看现有的意识理论是否适用于人工智能系统。对于人类或动物的意识，不存在公认的科学解释。 “意识本身是我们无法理解的东西，”谢夫林说。 “你永远不能排除新模型可能表现出类似情况的可能性。”他指出，虽然牡蛎可能没有“意识”，但如果我们发现新的证据，它们过着“令人惊奇、复杂的社会生活”，并且表现出比以前理解的要高得多的智力，那么它们的意识可能需要新的研究。

出于这个原因，在关于以我们给予其他生物的尊重和礼貌对待人工智能系统是对还是错的争论中，谢夫林采取了我们应该友善的立场。他引用了启蒙哲学家伊曼纽尔·康德的论点，即一个习惯虐待狗的人接下来可能会虐待人类。 “用户确实会对这些 [AI] 系统做出反应，包括我自己，通过某种方式将他们视为人类，”他说。

title: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
title_en: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
author: Manuel Uth
article_content:
Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.

Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,"he wrote in his announcement.

According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.

Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.

To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.

Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.

### Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof

Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement"on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

"It is all human, with no AI,"Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.

Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.

About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.),"Vakil wrote.

### Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next

Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification.

Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into 14 data packages.

Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.

Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.

This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems. In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations, which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results. Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.

### Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers

Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume,"Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.

### A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and push the math community into an identity crisis. Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."

article_content_zh:
Anthropic 的数学家 Levent Alpöge 周五表示，他使用大型语言模型来解决数学最著名的开放问题。

据《科学美国人》和其他美国媒体报道，阿尔波格在他的网站上发布了一篇论文和随附的计算机代码。 “我相信我已经与克劳德合作，发现了黎曼猜想的证明，”他在声明中写道。

根据 Alpöge 的说法，他的方法超越了原始的素数问题，还解决了广义黎曼假设 (GRH)，该假设将该排序原则扩展到一大堆相关方程。如果有更多的时间，他希望能够解决更广泛的扩展黎曼假设。

自大学以来，阿尔波格就将这个问题视为一个秘密的终生目标，预计需要几十年的时间才能解决。在过去的几个月里，他与 Anthropic 的人工智能模型密切合作，设定方向并将两种方法结合到一个简化的玩具模型上。一旦他们开始解决实际问题，人工智能就接管了任务，并将他远远抛在了终点线附近。

为了破解这个难题，两人借鉴了数学家斯捷潘诺夫的想法，后者在另一个数学系统中解决了类似的问题。该方法依赖于一种类似于高中微积分中平滑曲线求导的工具，这种技巧通常在整数上失败，因为单个值无法像连续线一样区分。

Alpöge 和 Claude 通过将特殊的数学变换像链接一样链接在一起来模仿导数的效果，从而绕过了这个障碍。语言模型提供了关键的见解，发现对于长度为 X 的数字序列，您需要链接与 X 的平方根一样多的变换。Alpöge 说，仅这样的想法就应该让其他数学家感到震惊。

### 斯坦福大学数学家们匆忙推出了全人类竞争证明

Alpöge 宣布这一消息几小时后，故事发生了戏剧性的转变。就在一次董事会会议之前，斯坦福大学数学教授兼美国数学会（AMS）主席拉维·瓦基尔（Ravi Vakil）在他的博客上发布了一个“仓促的公告”，分享了数学家亚历山德罗·马苏洛（Alessandro Masullo）撰写的广义黎曼猜想的独立证明草稿。

“这都是人类，没有人工智能，”瓦基尔写道。瓦基尔说，著名的斯坦福大学数论学家布莱恩·康拉德几个月来一直在悄悄审查马苏洛的工作，提供了广泛的反馈意见，目前这些反馈意见正在被纳入其中。

Masullo 原本应该在斯坦福大学花一年时间完善草案，然后再公开，但 Anthropic 突然宣布人工智能，迫使研究人员立即发布他们当前的版本。

在他最初宣布这一消息后大约八小时，瓦基尔更新了他的帖子，称有几个人联系了他，报告了拟议证明中的问题，这些问题是在不同人工智能模型的帮助下发现的。他说，特别是几位数学家首先提出了这些问题。 “像往常一样，所有问题都需要得到解决，让社区满意，然后这个证明才会被接受为真实的。（我不声明证明策略的正确性。）”Vakil 写道。

### 为什么这两个证明都成立以及接下来会发生什么

数学家们立即认真对待这两种说法，因为它们背后有基础。 Masullo 的传统证明经过 Brian Conrad 数月的审查，而 Alpöge 通过完整的计算机验证支持他的人工智能证明。

Alpöge 说，打印出来后，克劳德的论点将超过 250,000 页，因为人工智能甚至阐明了基本规则，例如二分之一以外的数字要么大于或小于二分之一。为了让数学家摆脱文字墙，Alpöge 仅以精益编程语言发布了证明，并将其分为 14 个数据包。

title: New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop
title_en: New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop

inline_images.caption: Inkling 2 Mini scores 20 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) and Nanbeige4.3-33B. With far fewer active parameters, the model sits directly on the Pareto frontier. | Image: Artificial Analysis
inline_images.caption_en: Inkling 2 Mini scores 20 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) and Nanbeige4.3-33B. With far fewer active parameters, the model sits directly on the Pareto frontier. | Image: Artificial Analysis

author: Matthias Bastian
article_content:
Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, a so-called looped transformer. A looped transformer runs certain layers multiple times for each token. Inkling 2 Mini runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row. That lets the model reason internally for longer without generating more text, finding the right answer with fewer tokens, according to Thinking Machines. The open mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters, with 5.4 billion active per token because of the loops, the company says. It processes text and images, has a 1-million-token context window, and is licensed under Apache 2.0.

Inkling 2 Mini leads all open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5 percent on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis gives it 20 points on its Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed.

Inkling 2 Mini runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia's DGX Spark. You can download the weights and a research version with variable loops from Hugging Face. It is also available to try in the Tinker Playground.

article_content_zh:
Thinking Machines 发布了 Inkling 2 Mini，即所谓的环形变压器。循环变压器为每个令牌多次运行某些层。 Inkling 2 Mini 连续运行 3 次，共运行 24 层中的 12 层。 Thinking Machines 表示，这使得模型可以在内部进行更长时间的推理，而无需生成更多文本，从而用更少的标记找到正确的答案。该公司表示，开放的专家混合模型有 264 亿个参数，由于存在循环，每个代币有 54 亿个活跃参数。它处理文本和图像，拥有 100 万个令牌上下文窗口，并获得 Apache 2.0 许可。

在代理编码测试中，Inkling 2 Mini 在 1000 亿个参数下领先于所有开放模型，在 DeepSWE v1.1 上得分为 48.2%，在 Vals Index v2.2 上得分为 46.5%。人工分析为其智能指数评分为 20 分，与 Qwen3.8 27B 持平，成本低约六倍，速度快四倍。

Inkling 2 Mini 可在内存至少为 32 GB 的 Mac 和 Nvidia 的 DGX Spark 上本地运行。您可以从 Hugging Face 下载权重和带有可变循环的研究版本。您也可以在 Tinker Playground 中尝试。

title: US technology stocks suffer their worst weekly loss since the pandemic as AI doubts pile up
title_en: US technology stocks suffer their worst weekly loss since the pandemic as AI doubts pile up
author: Matthias Bastian
article_content:
US tech stocks are tumbling. The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday and dropped 10.4 percent for the week, its worst showing since the Covid-19 crisis. That leaves the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear market territory, according to the Financial Times. Doubts over multibillion-dollar AI buildouts, the Nvidia scandal and questionable China deals, and political headwinds after Democrats' midterm win are driving the sell-off like a perfect storm.

title: Bytedance argues most AI training phases are unnecessary and backs it up with a competitive open model
title_en: Bytedance argues most AI training phases are unnecessary and backs it up with a competitive open model
author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
AI agents increasingly rely on complex training pipelines. A team from TikTok parent Bytedance and several US universities aims to show that three steps are enough.

AI models are expected to research the web on their own, run code, and solve multi-step tasks. According to a new paper, the training methods behind these capabilities are growing more and more nested, with many developers stacking numerous training phases one after another. The paper argues it's become almost impossible to tell which step actually helps, and reproducing the work is getting expensive.

title: The Race to Build a Quantum Computer Has Become a Sprint
title_en: The Race to Build a Quantum Computer Has Become a Sprint

inline_images.caption: Hartmut Neven, a physicist heading Google’s Quantum A.I. Lab in California, where he works on a kind of quantum computing involving neutral atoms, in which individual atoms are trapped with beams of light. (Ariana Drehsler for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Hartmut Neven, a physicist heading Google’s Quantum A.I. Lab in California, where he works on a kind of quantum computing involving neutral atoms, in which individual atoms are trapped with beams of light.

inline_images.caption: Dr. Lukin, with Ph.D. students in the basement lab. (Lucy Lu for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: Dr. Lukin, with Ph.D. students in the basement lab.

inline_images.caption: A quantum computer at Google’s Santa Barbara lab. (Adam Amengual for The New York Times)
inline_images.alt: A quantum computer at Google’s Santa Barbara lab.

author: Cade Metz
article_content:
For almost a decade, a Google lab in Santa Barbara, Calif., has led the global race to build a computer that harnesses the power of quantum mechanics: the unseen physical properties that allow light, subatomic particles and other exotic matter to behave in ways that defy common sense.

But this year, a brand-new lab in Colorado — developing a totally different path to a quantum machine — has changed the narrative and accelerated the competition.

The most surprising part of all is the new lab’s funder: Google itself.

Forty-five years after scientists first floated the idea of a quantum computer, the race to build one has turned into a sprint, with many experts now believing that the first viable machine could arrive before the end of the decade or soon after. This new excitement has unlocked enormous investment, with tech giants like Amazon, IBM and Microsoft racing alongside Google. In May, after China vowed to pump more than $15.2 billion into quantum research, the Trump administration fed $2 billion into a long line of American start-ups and chip makers.

But not all companies are approaching this big idea in the same way, and it is increasingly unclear which method will prevail — which is why Google has decided to hedge its bets.

To understand this twist, it’s necessary to go back to 2014, when Hartmut Neven, a German American physicist, founded the Google lab in Santa Barbara, hiring more than 20 scientists from the physics department at the University of California campus a few miles down the road.

Like several other tech giants, the Google scientists chose to build their quantum computer with a technology called a superconducting qubit, which relies on cooling metals to extremely low temperatures. And over the next five years, Google appeared to edge ahead of its rivals. In 2019, the company announced that its machine had achieved “quantum supremacy,” defined by the completion of a task that traditional computing couldn’t solve. In under four minutes, Google’s machine performed a calculation that would have taken an existing supercomputer 10,000 years.

Even as the field has progressed, one major hurdle to the creation of a usable quantum computer has remained: the problem of “error correction.” Error correction is an essential part of any computer, ensuring that calculations aren’t skewed by heat, electrical inference or other physical forces. The silicon microchips we use every day rely on robust electrical devices and sophisticated algorithms that eliminate such errors before they crash programs or corrupt data.

But the same methods of error correction used in conventional computing and communication don’t work with quantum computing. In recent years, even as Dr. Neven’s lab made progress on the problem, he began to see research from competitors using a totally different kind of quantum computing — the “neutral atoms” method, which involves trapping individual atoms with beams of light — that seemed to make error correction easier.

Faced with that research, Dr. Neven and Google took a bold step. In April, after a decade of investment in the Santa Barbara lab, the company opened a second, competing lab in Boulder, Colo., to explore neutral atom technology.

“Superconducting will get us there, but I wanted to avoid that last moment when some other technology might pass us by, even if it is only temporary, ” Dr. Neven said. “Neutral atoms have that chance.”

Dr. Neven is among the luminaries in the field who now think that powerful quantum computers are imminent. When they do emerge, they won’t replace the computers we rely on every day. But their facility with certain types of calculations could transform the world we live in — helping researchers discover new medicines, create new materials and accelerate the progress of artificial intelligence, among other things.

A quantum computer “can allow you to look at corners of the universe where you have never been,” said Mikhail Lukin, a physics professor at Harvard.

In the basement of the Harvard Physics Laboratory — a 100-year-old building in the North Yard of the university’s campus in Cambridge, Mass. — a door opens into a small room filled with computer screens, oscilloscopes, keyboards, surge protectors and a rat’s nest of electrical cables.

The floor is barely visible, mostly because the room is dominated by a rectangular enclosure surrounded on all four sides by a black curtain. As Dr. Lukin pulls back the curtain, he reveals a maze of lasers, lenses and mirrors designed to bounce beams of light into a tiny vacuum chamber in the middle of the enclosure. This is a quantum computer built from neutral atoms.

“See that little glow?” Dr. Lukin said, pointing to a nearby computer screen on which an optical microscope provided a live image from inside the tiny vacuum chamber. “That is a cloud of atoms.”

Traditional computers perform calculations by processing “bits” of information, with each bit holding either a 1 or a 0. Even the largest supercomputers, which span several buildings the size of football fields, operate in this simple way. But a quantum computer does not. It uses a new building block called a quantum bit, or qubit.

A qubit relies on superposition, a quantum-mechanical phenomenon that allows a single object to exist in multiple states — or even in multiple places — at the same time. By harnessing this strange behavior, a qubit can store a combination of 1 and 0 — two values held in the same place, at the same moment.

This means that two qubits can hold four values at once. Three qubits can hold eight values. And as the number of qubits grows, a quantum computer becomes exponentially more powerful than a traditional machine.

If this feels nonsensical, that is only natural. Famously, the Nobel Prize-winning physicist Richard Feynman once said, “Nobody understands quantum mechanics.” The point is: Quantum systems do not behave like objects encountered in everyday life.

Out in Santa Barbara, Google’s researchers have built qubits by cooling metals to temperatures near absolute zero. They wire these metals into microchips that look a lot like the ones sitting at the heart of conventional computers.

But here in the Harvard Physics Laboratory, Dr. Lukin and his colleagues lean on a very different process. Four floors below the Harvard Yard, they drop atoms of rubidium into a vacuum chamber, where lasers can slow the movement of these tiny objects and separate them from one another. These lasers can grab hold of each atom — like a pair of tweezers pinching a house fly — and carefully isolate it from the rest of the world.

As they do, each atom becomes a qubit. Dr. Lukin and his colleagues can perform calculations by manipulating these qubits, reading and writing information through subtle changes to their physical behavior. Much as a classical machine writes data into a bit by changing its charge, a quantum computer writes data into a qubit by shifting its quantum state.

The neutral atom technique is particularly effective because it gives researchers fine-grained control over each qubit. Because these atoms are neutral — because they are separated from the rest of the world — researchers can readily move them and manipulate them. Then, exploiting a phenomenon called the Rydberg blockade, individual atoms can be excited to high-energy states that let them trade information over long distances, without interacting with other atoms close by. This allows researchers to build the equivalent of circuits, capable of running complex calculations.

But arranging clouds of atoms into viable machines involves years of work. Dr. Lukin started working on the problem in the early 2000s, and the technology is only now reaching the point where it can start to realize its promise.

Dr. Lukin is also one of the founders and the chief scientist of the Cambridge start-up Quera, which aims to commercialize the technology. Increasingly, others are following his lead. In October, he attended the Nobel Symposium on Quantum Computing in Cape Town, where Jian-Wei Pan, widely known as China’s “father of quantum,” told him that no fewer than 20 Chinese companies were building machines using neutral atoms in the city of Shanghai alone.

“We have finally demonstrated all the elements that we need to get there,” Dr. Lukin said. “For the first time, the ideas that people had three or four decades ago are now within our line of sight.”

In Santa Barbara, Google’s quantum computer looks more like a Byzantine chandelier than a maze of lasers. This silver-and-gold lattice holds computer chips made from exotic metals that Dr. Neven and his team drop into massive refrigerators, cooling them to temperatures nearly 460 degrees below zero.

For years, these superconducting qubits looked like the surest path to a viable quantum computer. Like Amazon, IBM and others, Google strung together hundreds of qubits, showing that these quantum contraptions could perform increasingly complex calculations.

Google’s research indicates that a quantum computer is capable of the feats that scientists have promised for decades. But first, like all researchers in the field, they must solve the error correction problem.

Why is error correction so much harder in quantum computing than in traditional computing? Quantum systems are plagued by the famous “Heisenberg uncertainty principle,” which explains that with superposition — the state that quantum computers use to achieve their advantage over traditional machines — measuring one of the many properties of a particle will cause others to become unmeasurable. This means that merely looking at the information in an individual qubit causes it, in the terminology of quantum mechanics, to “collapse”: It slips back in the world of classical physics and transforms into an ordinary bit.

To deal with this problem, researchers design quantum computers that span far more qubits than they need for each calculation. That way, they can then read some qubits while leaving others undisturbed.

This is effective because quantum systems exhibit another strange property called “entanglement.” Through entanglement, one quantum system can influence the behavior of another, even when very far away — a phenomenon that Albert Einstein described as “spooky action at a distance.” Thanks to entanglement, researchers can glean information from a qubit by reading other qubits inside the same machine.

Part physical and part mathematical, this elaborate process is how researchers aim to crack error correction.

“It is intricate and complicated,” said Chris Langer, a fellow at Quantinuum, a company that is using a third quantum technique called “trapped ion” computing. “The basic idea is that you don’t measure the individual bits themselves. You measure information about the collection state.”

As far back as December 2024, Google said its machine had surpassed the “error correction threshold,” meaning that as its researchers increased the number of qubits, they could exponentially reduce the number of errors. Quantinuum recently showed similar progress with trapped ions — charged particles that researchers trap and isolate in much the same way they isolate neutral atoms. But other researchers argue that error correction could be most efficient with the neutral-atoms method, because it offers more freedom to rearrange the qubits, tinker with their behavior and make the process more efficient.

When you build a quantum computer from neutral atoms, you have more room to manipulate them, to move them from place to place, to reconfigure them into new logical circuits, said Adam Kaufman, a professor of physics at the University of Colorado, Boulder. That means you have more freedom to do error correction.

“You have a way of turning their interactions on and off,” Dr. Kaufman, who leads Google’s new team in Colorado, added. “This gives you the flexibility to realize a quantum circuit that you can rewire as you evolve your quantum computer over time.”

Dr. Neven still isn’t sure which method will reach the finish line first. Even if neutral atoms win the day, he believes, superconducting qubits will be more effective in the long run. Regardless, he has faith that Google is on track to solve the error correction problem in the coming years.

The result would be a machine that is nothing like today’s supercomputers. One long-feared consequence will be the breaking of today’s encryption technologies, which rely on huge factoring problems that quantum computers will, in theory, be able to solve; earlier this year, Google vowed to overhaul its encryption techniques before 2030.

“In 2022 or 2023, I would have a told you that the encryption scare was far out,” Dr. Neven said. “The timelines have come down.”

But such a machine will also provide a way of examining the world through the lens of quantum mechanics — helping to better understand biology and disease, the world around us and the ways we navigate that world. All are dependent on the strange behavior of the quantum realm.

If you want to build a computer that simulates the natural world and helps unlock its deepest mysteries, it must operate at a level that today’s computers do not, Dr. Feynman, the physicist, explained during a 1981 lecture. “Nature isn’t classical, dammit,” he said. “If you want to make a simulation of nature, you’d better make it quantum mechanical.”

title_zh: 谷歌量子计算战略从单一路径转向多线对冲
summary_zh: 谷歌通过在科罗拉多州新建实验室，并行开发不同技术路线，以应对量子纠错技术难题与日益激烈的全球算力竞赛
article_content_zh:
近十年来，位于加利福尼亚州圣巴巴拉的谷歌实验室一直引领着全球竞赛，打造一台利用量子力学力量的计算机：量子力学是一种看不见的物理特性，可以让光、亚原子粒子和其他奇异物质以违背常识的方式运行。

但今年，科罗拉多州的一个全新实验室正在开发一条完全不同的量子机器路径，改变了叙事并加速了竞争。

最令人惊讶的是新实验室的资助者：谷歌本身。

在科学家首次提出量子计算机的想法四十五年后，建造量子计算机的竞赛已经变成了冲刺，许多专家现在相信第一台可行的机器可能会在本世纪末或不久之后问世。这种新的兴奋释放了巨额投资，亚马逊、IBM 和微软等科技巨头与谷歌并肩作战。今年 5 月，在中国承诺向量子研究投入超过 152 亿美元后，特朗普政府向众多美国初创企业和芯片制造商注入了 20 亿美元。

但并非所有公司都以同样的方式实现这一伟大想法，而且越来越不清楚哪种方法会占上风——这就是谷歌决定对冲其赌注的原因。

要理解这种扭曲，有必要回到 2014 年，当时德裔美国物理学家哈特穆特·内文 (Hartmut Neven) 在圣巴巴拉建立了谷歌实验室，并从几英里外的加州大学校园物理系聘请了 20 多名科学家。

与其他几家科技巨头一样，谷歌科学家选择使用一种称为超导量子位的技术来构建他们的量子计算机，该技术依赖于将金属冷却到极低的温度。在接下来的五年里，谷歌似乎领先于竞争对手。 2019年，该公司宣布其机器已经实现了“量子霸权”，即完成了传统计算无法解决的任务。不到四分钟，谷歌的机器就完成了现有超级计算机需要一万年才能完成的计算。

即使该领域取得了进展，创建可用量子计算机的一个主要障碍仍然存在：“纠错”问题。纠错是任何计算机的重要组成部分，可确保计算不会因热、电推理或其他物理力而产生偏差。我们每天使用的硅微芯片依赖于强大的电气设备和复杂的算法，可以在此类错误导致程序崩溃或数据损坏之前消除这些错误。

但传统计算和通信中使用的相同纠错方法不适用于量子计算。近年来，尽管内文博士的实验室在这个问题上取得了进展，但他开始看到竞争对手的研究使用了一种完全不同的量子计算——“中性原子”方法，其中涉及用光束捕获单个原子——这似乎使纠错变得更容易。

面对这项研究，内文博士和谷歌迈出了大胆的一步。今年四月，在对圣巴巴拉实验室进行了十年的投资之后，该公司在科罗拉多州博尔德开设了第二个竞争实验室，以探索中性原子技术。

“超导将帮助我们实现这一目标，但我想避免最后一刻，因为其他技术可能会与我们擦肩而过，即使这只是暂时的，”内文博士说。 “中性原子就有这样的机会。”

内文博士是该领域的杰出人物之一，他们现在认为强大的量子计算机即将到来。当它们确实出现时，它们不会取代我们每天依赖的计算机。但它们具有某些类型计算的设施可以改变我们生活的世界——帮助研究人员发现新药物、创造新材料并加速人工智能的进步等。

哈佛大学物理学教授米哈伊尔·卢金 (Mikhail Lukin) 表示，量子计算机“可以让你看到从未去过的宇宙角落”。

哈佛物理实验室位于马萨诸塞州剑桥大学校园北院，是一栋拥有 100 年历史的建筑。在它的地下室里，一扇门通向一个小房间，里面装满了电脑屏幕、示波器、键盘、浪涌保护器和老鼠巢般的电缆。

title: NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge publish an AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup, saying it closes a loophole in OpenAI's solution (Peter Hall/Scientific American)
title_en: NYU's Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic's Levent Alpöge publish an AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup, saying it closes a loophole in OpenAI's solution (Peter Hall/Scientific American)

inline_images.caption: A visual representation of fluid dynamics. Researchers from New York University and Anthropic claimed to have solved the “real” version of the Navier-Stokes equ
inline_images.alt: A visual representation of fluid dynamics. Researchers from New York University and Anthropic claime

author: Scientific American
article_content:
Two months after getting scooped by OpenAI, N.Y.U. professor Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge are back with a new AI-aided proof of Navier-Stokes blowup

It looks like Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge was not satisfied with one blockbuster math proof today. Right after Alpöge’s announcement of a claimed proof of the Riemann hypothesis—math’s most famed open problem—has come the news that he and New York University professor Tristan Buckmaster believe they have closed a controversial loophole in OpenAI’s September solution of another million-dollar problem.

The Navier-Stokes equations, dating back to the early- to mid-19th century, model how fluids swirl and eddy. In September OpenAI proved that the equations “blow up,” meaning they occasionally claim that a fluid’s speed becomes infinite—something real fluids cannot do.

But while the September solution technically satisfied the conditions for the Clay Mathematics Institute’s $1-million prize, many experts were left unsatisfied with how it did so. OpenAI’s proof imagined an unrealistic, finely tuned force that “stirs” the liquid in just the right way to produce infinite velocity—an approach many consider a loophole in the wording of the problem.

The proof was also the subject of controversy because Buckmaster claimed it was a deliberate attempt on the part of OpenAI to scoop his and Alpöge’s progress on the problem. Buckmaster publicly aired his suspicions that the company even stole his user data in its mad race to beat him to the punch. (OpenAI denied allegations of foul play, and early reports suggest the company’s proof may have taken a different route to the solution than Buckmaster and Alpöge’s work.)

Now the pair claims to have taken back the lead on the problem, closing the loophole OpenAI left open and providing the solution to Navier-Stokes that experts have long sought.

On Mastodon at 8:37 A.M. EST this morning, Buckmaster posted a dense, artificial-intelligence-aided proof and noted that the write-up was unpolished because, “after last time,” he and Alpöge “couldn’t risk waiting” because of concerns over getting scooped. In the rush, the two also did not release the certificate of the result. In the report, they claimed it would be released soon.

Great science journalism requires human expertise, time, effort and creativity. And it costs money. That’s why I and the journalists here at Scientific American hope you’ll join our community.

title_zh: 纳维-斯托克斯方程解法争议升级
summary_zh: 纽约大学教授Buckmaster与Anthropic研究员Alpöge发布AI辅助证明，旨在修复OpenAI此前被指存在逻辑漏洞的流体力学解法
article_content_zh:
被 OpenAI 抢先两个月后，纽约大学 (N.Y.U.) Tristan Buckmaster 教授和 Anthropic 员工 Levent Alpöge 带着新的人工智能辅助的纳维-斯托克斯爆炸证明回来了

看来 Anthropic 员工 Levent Alpöge 对今天的一项重大数学证明并不满意。就在 Alpöge 宣布黎曼猜想（数学最著名的开放问题）的证明得到证明后，有消息称，他和纽约大学教授 Tristan Buckmaster 相信他们已经堵住了 OpenAI 9 月份解决另一个百万美元问题的一个有争议的漏洞。

纳维-斯托克斯方程可以追溯到 19 世纪早期到中期，它模拟了流体如何旋转和涡流。九月份，OpenAI 证明了这些方程“爆炸”，这意味着他们偶尔会声称流体的速度变得无限大——这是真实流体无法做到的。

尽管 9 月份的解决方案在技术上满足了克莱数学研究所 100 万美元奖金的条件，但许多专家对其实现方式并不满意。 OpenAI 的证明设想了一种不切实际的、经过微调的力，以正确的方式“搅拌”液体以产生无限的速度——许多人认为这种方法是问题措辞中的漏洞。

该证明也引起了争议，因为巴克马斯特声称这是 OpenAI 故意企图抢占他和 Alpöge 在该问题上的进展。巴克马斯特公开表示怀疑，该公司甚至在疯狂的竞赛中窃取了他的用户数据，以抢先一步。 （OpenAI 否认了犯规行为的指控，早期的报告表明该公司的证明可能采取了与 Buckmaster 和 Alpöge 的工作不同的途径来解决问题。）

现在，两人声称已经在这个问题上夺回了领先地位，堵住了 OpenAI 留下的漏洞，并为 Navier-Stokes 提供了专家们长期以来寻求的解决方案。

上午 8:37 在 Mastodon 上美国东部时间今天早上，巴克马斯特发布了一份密集的人工智能辅助证明，并指出该文章未经修饰，因为“在上次之后”，他和阿尔波格“不能冒险等待”，因为担心被抢先报道。仓促间，两人也没有公布成绩证明。他们在报告中声称很快就会发布。

伟大的科学新闻需要人类的专业知识、时间、努力和创造力。而且这需要花钱。这就是为什么我和《科学美国人》的记者希望您加入我们的社区。

title: Microsoft plans to retire its To Do app on June 30, 2027, offering migration to Planner for work and school accounts, but no replacement for personal accounts (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
title_en: Microsoft plans to retire its To Do app on June 30, 2027, offering migration to Planner for work and school accounts, but no replacement for personal accounts (Todd Bishop/GeekWire)
author: GeekWire
article_content:
Microsoft acquired the popular Wunderlist app in 2015, shut it down in 2020 and told its loyal users that Microsoft To Do would be their new home. Now they’re being asked to pack up again.

Microsoft plans to retire the To Do apps on June 30, 2027, moving personal task management for work and school accounts into Planner, its team project-management app. Microsoft disclosed the change Wednesday in a long Planner blog post amid the company’s Ignite announcements, and Windows Latest flagged the change later that day.

The reaction was swift and mostly unhappy. Tom Warren of The Verge summed it up on X: “Microsoft is killing its great tasks app in favor of its worse tasks app.”

That’s not entirely fair to Planner, which is built for a different job. But it captures the gripe: To Do was simple, free and worked across Windows, Mac, iOS, Android and the web, and nothing Microsoft is offering replaces all of that.

The catch for personal users: Microsoft’s support page says the To Do apps are also retiring for personal Microsoft accounts, including paid Microsoft 365 Personal and Family subscribers, and that Planner isn’t available for those accounts. Microsoft hasn’t announced a replacement for them.

For work and school accounts, Microsoft says Planner “will be the destination for managing personal work tasks,” but “existing To Do tasks and lists will not migrate to Planner.” It says it will offer a way to export To Do data before the app shuts down.

Tony Redmond of Office365itpros, who tracks Microsoft 365 closely, cataloged the gaps: no file attachments on private Planner tasks, no equivalent for To Do’s list groups, no transfer of shared-list membership, assignments or permissions, and no native Planner apps for Windows or Mac.

He also noted the irony that Outlook’s old Exchange-based tasks will outlive To Do.

Why Microsoft is doing it: The company said putting individual and shared work on the same foundation lets it deliver more consistent features, and lets people connect their own tasks to Copilot and other AI agents. A new Planner agent, available with a Copilot add-on license, can take on tasks and generate status reports.

The Register’s Richard Speed put it less charitably, saying Microsoft had slipped the news into “this week’s Ignite AI puffery.”

Users weigh in: Brad Silverberg, the former Microsoft executive who led Windows 95 development and later became a Seattle venture investor, posted on X that he has used To Do daily, and Wunderlist before it.

“Very disappointed now,” he wrote, adding that he’s looking at TickTick and Todoist.

Similar posts piled up on LinkedIn from Microsoft 365 consultants and everyday users, some of them describing Planner as clunky by comparison.

Patrick Husting, a Seattle-area entrepreneur and software developer whose Ghostwriter add-in brought AI to Microsoft Office before Microsoft announced Microsoft 365 Copilot, offered on LinkedIn to maintain To Do for Microsoft for free.

Rivals smell an opportunity: Competitors wasted no time. TickTick posted a migration guide for To Do refugees. Todoist CEO Amir Salihefendic wrote on LinkedIn that the shutdown was “pretty unexpected” and pointed out that his app has outlasted competitors for 20 years.

The most pointed pitch came from Superlist, which called itself “the natural successor” and said it already has a tool for importing To Do lists. Wunderlist founder Christian Reber started the company in 2020.

Reber and his co-founders sold Wunderlist’s parent company, 6Wunderkinder, to Microsoft in 2015 for a reported $100 million to $200 million. In 2019, as Microsoft prepared to shut the app down, he publicly asked Satya Nadella to sell it back. Microsoft kept it, then retired it in favor of To Do.

Now some of those former Wunderlist users may end up back with the people who built it.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

Learn more about the technology making it all work.

So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next

The AWS re:Invent livestream runs November 29–December 3, so you can follow the week from wherever you are. Choose from 60+ sessions across topics and skill levels, from introductory overviews to advanced deep dives. Catch every major launch as it is announced. Customers share what they learned, and select sessions include live Q&A. Livestream registration is free.

article_content_zh:
微软于 2015 年收购了广受欢迎的奇妙清单应用程序，并于 2020 年将其关闭，并告诉其忠实用户微软待办将成为他们的新家。现在他们又被要求收拾行李。

微软计划于 2027 年 6 月 30 日停用待办事项应用程序，将工作和学校帐户的个人任务管理转移到其团队项目管理应用程序 Planner 中。周三，微软在公司发布 Ignite 公告的同时，在一篇长篇 Planner 博客文章中披露了这一变化，Windows Last 也在当天晚些时候标记了这一变化。

人们的反应很快，而且大多是不高兴的。 The Verge 的 Tom Warren 对 X 进行了总结：“微软正在淘汰其优秀的任务应用程序，转而选择更糟糕的任务应用程序。”

这对于 Planner 来说并不完全公平，因为它是为不同的工作而构建的。但它抓住了人们的抱怨：To Do 简单、免费，并且可以在 Windows、Mac、iOS、Android 和网络上运行，而微软提供的任何产品都无法取代这一切。

个人用户面临的问题：微软的支持页面称，个人微软帐户的待办事项应用程序也将停用，包括付费的 Microsoft 365 个人和家庭订阅者，并且 Planner 不适用于这些帐户。微软尚未宣布它们的替代品。

对于工作和学校帐户，微软表示 Planner“将成为管理个人工作任务的目的地”，但“现有的待办事项和列表不会迁移到 Planner。”它表示它将提供一种在应用程序关闭之前导出待办事项数据的方法。

Office365itpros 的托尼·雷蒙德 (Tony Redmond) 密切跟踪 Microsoft 365，他对这些差距进行了分类：私人 Planner 任务上没有文件附件，待办事项列表组没有等效项，没有共享列表成员身份、分配或权限的传输，并且没有适用于 Windows 或 Mac 的本机 Planner 应用程序。

他还指出具有讽刺意味的是，Outlook 旧的基于 Exchange 的任务将比待办事项更长寿。

微软这样做的原因：该公司表示，将个人和共享工作放在同一基础上可以提供更一致的功能，并让人们将自己的任务连接到 Copilot 和其他人工智能代理。带有 Copilot 附加许可证的新 Planner 代理可以承担任务并生成状态报告。

The Register 的理查德·斯皮德 (Richard Speed) 的说法就不那么仁慈了，他说微软已经将这一消息塞进了“本周的 Ignite AI 吹嘘”中。

用户发表意见：领导 Windows 95 开发、后来成为西雅图风险投资人的微软前高管布拉德·西尔弗伯格 (Brad Silverberg) 在 X 上发帖称，他曾使用过“待办事项”和之前的奇妙清单。

“现在非常失望，”他写道，并补充说他正在考虑 TickTick 和 Todoist。

Microsoft 365 顾问和日常用户在 LinkedIn 上发布了类似的帖子，其中一些人认为相比之下，Planner 很笨重。

Patrick Husting 是一位西雅图地区的企业家和软件开发人员，他的 Ghostwriter 插件在 Microsoft 发布 Microsoft 365 Copilot 之前将 AI 引入了 Microsoft Office，并在 LinkedIn 上免费提供 Microsoft 待办事项维护服务。

author: Nikkei Asia
article_content:
TAIPEI -- Tighter U.S. export controls introduced Thursday are having a far broader impact on the global semiconductor supply chain than initially expected, extending beyond advanced AI chips to those used in everyday mobile and consumer applications and affecting developers beyond China, multiple industry executives told Nikkei Asia.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker, has put shipments to several Chinese and non-Chinese chip developers on hold as it reviews compliance with the stricter regulations, sources briefed on the matter said.

The new rules, announced Monday by the U.S. Commerce Department, further restrict foundries' ability to serve Chinese chip developers, including Xiaomi, as well as customers in Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore and other countries. They threaten emerging semiconductor ambitions across Asia and disrupt the global chip supply chain on a much wider scale than previously, Nikkei Asia has learned.

Contract chipmakers must now assume that all chips manufactured using process technologies more advanced than the 14- or 16-nanometer nodes first mass-produced by TSMC and Samsung Electronics about a decade ago are subject to export restrictions, unless their developers are on a U.S. government whitelist. The rules could therefore affect a broad range of chips, including those used in autonomous driving, connectivity and smartphones, rather than just high-performance processors for data center servers.

briefed on the matter said the new rules effectively required Chinese chip developers to apply for export licenses, even for chips designed for consumer electronics and automotive applications. Some key TSMC clients, including Xiaomi, which is developing its own mobile processors, and many Chinese automotive chip developers, are affected, two sources told Nikkei Asia.

"The new rule is very strict this time, and the affecting scope is far beyond only chips for data centers but covers smartphone processors, autonomous driving and other types of chips for consumer electronics as well as others if they are using nodes that are 14-nanometer or 16-nanometer or more advanced tech," a source said.

"The move would delay shipments to many chip developers worldwide before they can clear compliance and hit many emerging startups in many Asian nations."

Previous U.S. restrictions primarily targeted data center and high-performance computing chips that met certain thresholds and used advanced packaging technologies required for AI computing.

However, the latest restrictions could also deal a blow to emerging chip design hubs across Asia that are seeking to build their own chip development ecosystems. These include Vietnam and Malaysia, both of which have ambitions to develop domestic chip design capabilities.

As part of the latest restrictions, the U.S. has also said global contract chipmakers and chip packaging service providers need to do more to verify the final destinations of the chips.

The export controls aim to close loopholes that have allowed Chinese chip developers and other entities to continue accessing the world's leading semiconductor supply chains and advanced American technologies. The same controls also require data centers in Malaysia, Singapore, and Thailand to apply for U.S. licenses.

TSMC said it was aware of the new regulations and would comply as applicable. Xiaomi did not immediately respond to Nikkei Asia's request for comment.

The Financial Times first reported TSMC and Samsung Electronics had suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers.

article_content_zh:
台北——多位行业高管告诉《日经亚洲》，美国周四实施的更严格的出口管制对全球半导体供应链的影响比最初预期的要广泛得多，不仅限于先进的人工智能芯片，还扩展到日常移动和消费应用中使用的芯片，并影响到中国以外的开发商。

全球最大的代工芯片制造商台积电已暂停向多家中国和非中国芯片开发商发货，以审查是否遵守更严格的规定。

美国商务部周一宣布的新规定进一步限制了代工厂为包括小米在内的中国芯片开发商以及越南、马来西亚、新加坡和其他国家的客户提供服务的能力。日经亚洲获悉，它们威胁到整个亚洲新兴的半导体雄心，并比以前更广泛地扰乱全球芯片供应链。

合同芯片制造商现在必须假设，所有使用比台积电和三星电子大约十年前首次大规模生产的 14 或 16 纳米节点更先进的工艺技术制造的芯片都受到出口限制，除非其开发商列入美国政府白名单。因此，这些规则可能会影响广泛的芯片，包括用于自动驾驶、连接和智能手机的芯片，而不仅仅是数据中心服务器的高性能处理器。

了解此事的消息人士称，新规定实际上要求中国芯片开发商申请出口许可证，即使是为消费电子和汽车应用设计的芯片。两位消息人士告诉《日经亚洲》，台积电的一些主要客户，包括正在开发自己的移动处理器的小米，以及许多中国汽车芯片开发商，都受到了影响。

消息人士称：“这次新规定非常严格，影响范围远远超出了数据中心芯片的范围，还包括智能手机处理器、自动驾驶和其他类型的消费电子芯片，以及其他使用14纳米、16纳米或更先进技术节点的芯片。”

“此举将推迟向全球许多芯片开发商发货，然后他们才能通过合规性并打击许多亚洲国家的许多新兴初创公司。”

美国此前的限制主要针对数据中心和满足一定门槛并使用人工智能计算所需的先进封装技术的高性能计算芯片。

然而，最新的限制也可能对亚洲各地正在寻求建立自己的芯片开发生态系统的新兴芯片设计中心造成打击。其中包括越南和马来西亚，这两个国家都有发展国内芯片设计能力的雄心。

作为最新限制的一部分，美国还表示，全球合约芯片制造商和芯片封装服务提供商需要采取更多措施来验证芯片的最终目的地。

出口管制旨在弥补漏洞，这些漏洞使中国芯片开发商和其他实体能够继续获得世界领先的半导体供应链和先进的美国技术。同样的控制还要求马来西亚、新加坡和泰国的数据中心申请美国许可证。

台积电表示已了解新规定，并将酌情遵守。小米没有立即回应日经亚洲的置评请求。

英国《金融时报》首先报道称，台积电和三星电子已暂停向中国客户发货部分芯片。

title: Ubisoft launches Motherbrain, a subsidiary focused on developing "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds" (Sophie McEvoy/GamesIndustry.biz)
title_en: Ubisoft launches Motherbrain, a subsidiary focused on developing "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds" (Sophie McEvoy/GamesIndustry.biz)
author: GamesIndustry.biz
article_content:
Ubisoft has launched Motherbrain, a dedicated subsidiary focused on developing proprietary generative AI technology for gameplay.

Announced in the firm's H1 financial results published yesterday, Motherbrain consists of the team behind Ubisoft's generative AI project Teammates, which began playtesting last year.

Ubisoft said the subsidiary is currently focused on developing "smart NPCs with memory and AI game masters that manage large-scale systemic worlds."

"[Motherbrain] aims to serve creators globally, both within Ubisoft’s Creative House ecosystem and beyond, and form partnerships with selected technology actors."

Ubisoft CEO Yves Guillemot added that Motherbrain aimed to "empower creators and open up new possibilities for richer, more immersive and engaging player experiences."

The launch of Motherbrain comes as Ubisoft laid off 166 staff at its Montreal and Quebec studios. Production and support roles were eliminated "to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs."

As GamesIndustry.biz understands, the cuts accounted for less than 4% of the studios' total headcount and included members of Vantage Studios.

"As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs," said Ubisoft.

article_content_zh:
育碧推出了 Motherbrain，这是一家专注于开发专有的游戏生成人工智能技术的子公司。

该公司在昨天发布的上半年财务业绩中宣布，Motherbrain 由育碧生成式人工智能项目 Teammates 背后的团队组成，该项目于去年开始进行游戏测试。

育碧表示，该子公司目前专注于开发“具有记忆能力的智能 NPC 和管理大规模系统世界的人工智能游戏大师”。

“[Motherbrain] 旨在为育碧 Creative House 生态系统内外的全球创作者提供服务，并与选定的技术参与者建立合作伙伴关系。”

育碧首席执行官 Yves Guillemot 补充道，Motherbrain 的目标是“为创作者赋能，并为更丰富、更身临其境和更具吸引力的玩家体验开辟新的可能性”。

《Motherbrain》推出之际，育碧解雇了蒙特利尔和魁北克工作室的 166 名员工。生产和支持角色被取消，“以确保我们的资源与当前的生产优先事项和业务需求保持一致。”

据GamesIndustry.biz了解，裁员人数占工作室总人数的不到4%，其中包括Vantage Studios的成员。

育碧表示：“随着我们产品组合的发展，我们的制作需求也在发生变化，这要求我们调整一些团队的规模，以确保我们的资源与当前的制作优先事项和业务需求保持一致。”

title: Sources: the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its NCIC database, which is used by law enforcement to share info on warrants and background checks (Evan Perez/CNN)
title_en: Sources: the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its NCIC database, which is used by law enforcement to share info on warrants and background checks (Evan Perez/CNN)

inline_images.caption: Evan Perez
inline_images.alt: Evan Perez

inline_images.caption: A seal reading
inline_images.alt: A seal reading

author: CNN
article_content:
The FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database that serves as a lifeline between federal, state and local law enforcement, two people briefed on the investigation said. The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers is the second such breach in recent months.

The NCIC database is used by law enforcement nationwide to share information on warrants and background checks. The discovery of the latest intrusion in recent days comes as the Trump administration has sought to assuage public concern about the nation’s cybersecurity amid a series of high profile outages affecting banks, the National Security Agency and the FAA’s air traffic control system.

The FBI didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. On Thursday, after bureau officials learned of the latest cybersecurity incident, FBI Director Kash Patel appeared on Fox News to tout the FBI’s cybersecurity work. Patel used the appearance to discuss an operation completed months ago aimed at urging companies to update their systems and prevent hackers from getting to their sensitive data.

Patel referred to Operation Winter Shield as if it was still in the works, and touted the current administration for making updates to key systems to protect the nation’s critical infrastructure. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said. “We are staying ahead of the curve and making up for lost time.” Prior hacks A September attack by a group called ShinyHunters targeted sensitive employee personal data from an FBI jobs website.

A Canadian cybersecurity researcher and author has been arrested and faces charges related to the ShinyHunters breach. After the ShinyHunters breach, some FBI employees felt left in the dark about whether they were affected by the data theft and underwhelmed by the security resources being offered to victims, CNN previously reported.

In an earlier breach in 2023, hackers breached a computer system the FBI’s New York field office used in child sexual exploitation investigations, including a system used to store images related to the Jeffrey Epstein probe, CNN previously reported. CNN’s Sean Lyngaas contributed to this report.

article_content_zh:
两名了解调查情况的人士表示，联邦调查局正在调查其全国犯罪信息数据库明显遭到破坏的事件，该数据库是联邦、州和地方执法部门之间的生命线。明显的黑客入侵国家犯罪信息中心是近几个月来第二起此类违规事件。

NCIC 数据库被全国执法部门用来共享逮捕令和背景调查的信息。最近几天发现最新的入侵事件之际，特朗普政府试图缓解公众对国家网络安全的担忧，因为一系列引人注目的网络中断影响了银行、国家安全局和美国联邦航空局的空中交通管制系统。

联邦调查局没有立即回应置评请求。周四，在联邦调查局官员获悉最新的网络安全事件后，联邦调查局局长卡什·帕特尔出现在福克斯新闻节目中，宣传联邦调查局的网络安全工作。帕特尔借此机会讨论了几个月前完成的一项行动，旨在敦促公司更新其系统并防止黑客获取其敏感数据。

帕特尔提到“冬季盾牌行动”时就好像它仍在进行中一样，并称赞现任政府对关键系统进行了更新以保护国家的关键基础设施。 “其他政府本可以进行这些更新，但他们没有，”他说。 “我们保持领先地位并弥补失去的时间。”之前的黑客攻击 一个名为 ShinyHunters 的组织 9 月份发起的攻击针对的是 FBI 招聘网站上的敏感员工个人数据。

一名加拿大网络安全研究人员和作家已被捕，并面临与 ShinyHunters 数据泄露相关的指控。据美国有线电视新闻网 (CNN) 此前报道，在 ShinyHunters 事件发生后，一些联邦调查局 (FBI) 员工对自己是否受到数据盗窃的影响一无所知，并对向受害者提供的安全资源感到失望。

据美国有线电视新闻网 (CNN) 此前报道，在 2023 年早些时候的一次泄露中，黑客入侵了联邦调查局纽约办事处用于儿童性剥削调查的计算机系统，其中包括用于存储与杰弗里·爱泼斯坦调查相关的图像的系统。美国有线电视新闻网 (CNN) 的肖恩·林格斯 (Sean Lyngaas) 对本报告做出了贡献。

【起因与机理】作为执法部门信息共享核心，系统安全性的丧失威胁到全美司法与执法联动效能
【调查与监管诉求】FBI NCIC执法数据库发生严重安全入侵。
【各方立场与态度】此前已发生过针对FBI招聘网站及纽约分局案件库的泄露事件。
